Tensions ease after PPP man prevails in Diamer re-polling
items.description: • Consolidated results finally issued after over 24-hour delay • PPP, IPP supporters blocked KKH in Diamer for 10 hours GILGIT: A controversy over re-polling in Gilgit-Baltistan Assem­bly constituency GBA-16 Diamer-II was finally put to rest on Monday night, after the GB Election Commission declared PPP candidate Attaullah Shah as victorious, with a margin of 85 votes. According to the final consolidated result (Form 49), he secured 6,758 votes against 6,673 garnered by his rival, Imam Malik of the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party (IPP). Re-polling at three polling stations was completed on Sunday. However, official Form 47 results for two stations were not issued until Monday night. It may be recalled that Mr Malik had contested GB Assembly general elections as an independent candidate, but later joined the IPP. Earlier in the day, supporters of both men had blocked the Kara­koram Highway (KKH) at different locations in Diamer for around 10 hours, amid claims of rigging and irregularities in the polls. Police also claimed to have rec­overed a ballot box allegedly snat­ched from the Wora female polling station. However, polling and counting at the Wora female polling station remained incomplete amid reports of ballot boxes being snatched. Counting at the combined male and female polling station in Gechi was completed. According to Form 45, PPP candidate Attaullah Shah secured 427 votes, while IPP candidate Imam Malik received 53. The unofficial results of the Sarai female polling station showed that Mr Malik secured 295 votes, while Mr Shah received 145 votes. Mr Shah’s supporters staged a protest in Gechi and blocked the KKH, demanding the issuance of official results for the two disputed polling stations. They called for the results to be declared without including the votes in the allegedly snatched ballot boxes. Addressing his supporters on Monday, Mr Shah said it was unjust that the results had not been announced despite his apparent victory. He said he had been struggling for the past six months and that his electoral right had been denied despite repolling, alleged rigging and other malpractices. He said ballot boxes from the Wora female polling station had been snatched on Sunday evening and returned after 10 hours, but the authorities were now seeking to include their votes in the counting process Mr Malik’s supporters also blocked the KKH in Chilas, demanding that a recovered ballot box from the Wora polling station be included in the counting process. Addressing the protesters, Mr Malik claimed that counting at the Wora polling station had been completed in the presence of police and polling staff. He said the results showed that he had secured 700 votes and won the election with a lead of 500 votes. Earlier on Monday, Chief Election Commissioner Raja Shahbaz Khan said he had sought reports from the district returning officer, returning officer and inspector general of police regarding the law and order situation that erupted at polling stations in Diamer on Sunday. He said the election code of conduct had been issued to both parties ahead of repolling and warned that strict action would be taken against anyone found responsible for violating it. Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

items.title: Stay away from tomorrow’s APC campaign rally, Itsekiri youths warn Oborevwori
items.description: By Jimitota Onoyume Some youths under the aegis of Itsekiri ethnic nationality have advised Itsekiri political leaders and governor of the state, Sheriff Oborevwori to stay away from the forthcoming campaign rally of the All Progressives Congress, APC, scheduled to hold at Nana College on Wednesday. In a statement online by Appearance Efejuku and Joseph Okotie, the youths said their position was necessitated by the rejection of what they described as the alleged fraudulent ward structure delineation in Warri South Local Government Area, adding that Itsekiri political leaders who choose to attend the rally would be labeled enemies of the ethnic nation. The statement further advised Governor Oborevwori and his political allies to stay away from the campaign until the legitimate concern raised by the Itsekiri people on the issues were addressed. The statemtnt said: The general youths of Warri Kingdom and the Itsekiri people hereby advise all Itsekiri political leaders, elected and appointed office holders, and stakeholders to boycott the forthcoming APC campaign scheduled to hold at Nana College on Wednesday. According to the statement, “This position is necessitated by the rejection of the fraudulent ward structure delineation in Warri South council. “We further advise the state governor and his political allies to stay away from the said campaign until this legitimate concern is addressed. “For the avoidance of doubt, any Itsekiri son or daughter who chooses to participate in the campaign against this collective position will be treated as an enemy of Itsekiri Nation. Our position is clear: No legitimate ward structure, no political participation.” The post Stay away from tomorrow’s APC campaign rally, Itsekiri youths warn Oborevwori appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Raised temperatures
items.description: IT seems one of the government’s main coalition partners is becoming increasingly apprehensive about the measures being used to muzzle dissent. In a recent phone call with JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari strongly condemned “the government’s actions and political vengeance” targeting the maulana’s party. He reportedly chided the government for being intolerant of criticism, while acknowledging that the opposition plays an “extremely important role in democracy and the parliamentary system”. During the conversation, he is also said to have expressed the view that the government should “refrain from such actions that weaken democracy and parliament.” The PPP chairman, it seems, wants to distance his party from the policies of the ruling PML-N. In recent weeks, he has urged his coalition partners to adopt a more conciliatory approach towards opposition parties and seek a national political reset . More cynical observers will describe this as buyer’s remorse. After all, one of the main reasons for the JUI-F’s discontent is the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP. The order to impose those was signed, of course, by the co-chairperson of the PPP, President Asif Ali Zardari, despite many warnings that it would only complicate the country’s political crisis. Ever since he took an adversarial stance on the matter — a position precipitated by the government scuttling his efforts to mediate between it and the opposition parties — Mr Rehman has suddenly run into several ‘difficulties’. He has alleged that drones have been hovering over his home, and that his sons and other party leaders are being harassed by NAB. Several JUI-F leaders have also become the subject of smear videos online. His party is now taking to the streets to protest. The opposition is not an inconvenience to be managed, as Mr Bhutto-Zardari rightly pointed out. It is integral to the parliamentary system. When politicians suddenly face accountability after running into political disputes, questions arise about institutional credibility. The government, too, loses the moral authority it needs to rally the country against real threats. KP remains in the grip of a militant surge, and the federal government had justified its takeover of the province with the promise that it would stabilise it. The last thing that province needs is a fresh front of agitation, with yet another party on the streets while the security forces are under constant attack. What the country needs is for political temperatures to come down. The government should end its pressure tactics and open channels to the opposition. Disputes between political parties must be settled in parliament and at the negotiating table, not on the streets. Published in Dawn, November 17th, 2026

items.title: Israeli leaders slam Netanyahu’s ‘attempted election coup’
items.description: • Reports say PM’s office ‘tried to frame’ Arab-Israeli party members on eve of polls; three freed as allegations prove baseless • Attorney general blocks Shin Bet bid to wiretap Joint List leaders • Opposition calls for probe JERUSALEM: Israeli opposition leaders denou­nced on Monday what they called an “attempted coup” following reports that outgoing Prime Minis­­ter Ben­jamin Netanyahu’s office tried to frame members of an Arab-Israeli party ahead of recent elections. “As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear: this wasn’t an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup,” Yair Lapid, who headed the opposition in the previous legislature, wrote on X. Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Sunday that on the eve of the Oct 27 election, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, phoned in a complaint to police about members of the Arab-Israeli Raam party. Norden reportedly direc­ted police to a purported intelligence source — a former employee of Neta­n­­yahu’s office — whose information led to the arrest of three Raam members. The three men were later released after police determined the allegatio­­ns were unfounded. Net­­anyahu subsequently accu­­sed Arab parties of electoral fraud after they won a record number of seats. The Israeli newspaper Haaretz also reported that David Zini, head of the Shin Bet domestic securi­ty service, sought to wiretap leaders of the Joint List, the other Arab grouping, but the attorney general denied the request for lack of evidence. In response to the rep­orting and political criticism, the Israeli police have said they will “re­­v­iew the decision-making and information-transmission process”. Following the reports, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen also called the allegations an “attempted coup by Netanyahu”, writing on X that if confirmed, “this is a criminal mechanism that operated from the heart of government to rig the election results”. Raam’s number two, Yoav Segalovitz, deman­ded an urgent criminal investigation, saying Netanyahu “cried out that his election was being stolen, while he himself tried to steal the country”. Netanyahu’s Likud party called the reports “utterly absurd” and claimed they were aimed at blocking a national unity government. Netanyahu’s main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, wrote on Sunday that the caretaker prime minister “can­not remain at the head of the government for a minute longer” and demanded an investigation. He said the affair demonstrated that the caretaker prime minister was “a concrete, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy”. Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot’s opposition secured the 61-seat majority needed to govern after last month’s vote. Both Raam and the Joint List have indicated they support Eisenkot. Published in Dawn, November 17th, 2026

items.title: Forum Mondial des Femmes pour la Paix : Essaouira clôture trois jours de dialogue et d’engagement
items.description: La troisième édition du Forum Mondial des Femmes pour la Paix s’est achevée samedi 14 novembre à Essaouira, après trois jours consacrés au dialogue, à la diplomatie, à la culture et à l’engagement des femmes en faveur de la paix. Près de 500 participants, venus notamment de zones de conflit, ont pris part à ce rendez-vous porté par le mouvement des Guerrières de la Paix, nommé au Prix Nobel de la Paix 2025. Du 12 au 14 novembre, la cité des Alizés a accueilli militantes, personnalités politiques, diplomates, représentants d’organisations internationales, artistes et acteurs de la société civile autour d’une même ambition : faire émerger de nouvelles voies pour construire une paix durable. Entre témoignages, tables rondes, rencontres et moments artistiques, le forum a placé le dialogue entre les peuples et les cultures au cœur de ses échanges. La cérémonie d’ouverture, organisée jeudi 12 novembre à Bayt Dakira, a réuni notamment André Azoulay, Conseiller du Roi Mohammed VI, Tarik Ottmani, maire d’Essaouira, et Ibrahim Kazam, maire d’Abu Gosh. Parmi les premiers temps forts, la table ronde consacrée à la culture et à la paix a réuni la chanteuse Yael Naim, le peintre marocain Mohamed Mourabiti, l’actrice et dramaturge Séphora Haymann ainsi que l’écrivaine et sociologue franco-iranienne Saena Delacroix-Sadighiyan. Les échanges ont notamment mis en avant le rôle de l’art dans la construction de nouveaux récits favorables au dialogue et à la paix. Vendredi 13 novembre, la question de la diplomatie féministe a également occupé une place centrale. Isabelle Rome, Ghadir Hani, Céline Bardet et Yasmina Asrarguis ont échangé sur la place des femmes dans les processus de construction de la paix et sur la nécessité d’une diplomatie davantage inclusive. Diplomatie et société civile réunies à Essaouira Autre moment fort de cette troisième édition : le panel ministériel organisé à Dar Souiri. Celui-ci a réuni Nasser Bourita, ministre marocain des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération africaine et des Marocains résidant à l’étranger, et Jean-Noël Barrot, ministre français de l’Europe et des Affaires étrangères, aux côtés de plusieurs militants engagés pour la paix, parmi lesquels Ali Abu Awwad, Maya Savir, Amal Abed et Yonathan Hefetz. Cette rencontre a permis de croiser les regards de la diplomatie et ceux des acteurs de terrain, directement engagés dans les initiatives de paix. Les discussions consacrées à la lutte contre la haine en ligne et au rôle de la jeunesse ont, par ailleurs, souligné les nouveaux défis liés au numérique et l’importance d’impliquer les jeunes générations dans les initiatives de paix. Le volet culturel a occupé une place importante durant le forum. L’exposition « Itinéraire pour la Paix », inaugurée au Bastion d’Essaouira, a proposé une immersion dans l’univers des Guerrières de la Paix à travers des portraits photographiques, des témoignages et des œuvres de Leïla Alaoui et de Gerda Hegedüs. Des lectures musicales et plusieurs performances artistiques, notamment de Yael Naim et Gildaa, sont venues prolonger les échanges. La programmation culturelle s’est poursuivie avec la présentation de projets éditoriaux des Éditions Ana Mogador ainsi qu’avec la projection de Résister pour la Paix de Hanna Assouline et Sonia Terrab, suivie de Mother's Call, porté avec Women Wage Peace et Women of the Sun. Le forum s’est finalement clôturé en musique, samedi 14 novembre, avec la chanteuse Juliata Cohen à la Médiathèque d’Essaouira. Un appel international porté par des femmes venues de zones de conflit L’un des moments les plus marquants de cette édition a été l’Appel international des femmes pour la paix, porté par plusieurs militantes venues de différents pays, notamment Mayada Adil du Soudan, Aida Tavakoli d’Iran, Fatemeh Jailani d’Afghanistan, Ghita El Khyari du Maroc, Esther Omam du Cameroun, Naama Lazimi d’Israël et Ghadir Hani de Palestine/Israël. Réunies sur scène, elles ont lancé un appel à la communauté internationale et rappelé que la paix repose sur une mobilisation collective et sur la capacité à faire dialoguer des voix issues de contextes différents. À travers cette troisième édition, Essaouira s’est ainsi affirmée comme un espace de rencontre entre diplomatie, société civile, culture et engagement citoyen, avec les femmes au centre des réflexions sur les voies possibles vers une paix durable. Porté par les Guerrières de la Paix, mouvement international réunissant militantes, artistes, intellectuelles et personnalités politiques, le Forum Mondial des Femmes pour la Paix entend poursuivre cette dynamique en faisant du dialogue et de la transmission des expériences des leviers essentiels de construction de la paix. The post Forum Mondial des Femmes pour la Paix : Essaouira clôture trois jours de dialogue et d’engagement appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: ‘Teachers, doctors won’t pay tax when I become gov’
items.description: By Cynthia Alo & Kafayat Kokumo LAGOS—Lagos State governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, Mr. Adedeji Doherty, yesterday, promised to exempt teachers and doctors from paying taxes, if elected governor, saying his administration will use increased Federal allocations to improve healthcare, education and welfare of residents. Doherty, who made the promise during an interview on a Channels Television programme, said he would also introduce a tax card that would enable residents unable to afford the existing tax burden to pay N10,000 annually and enjoy subsidies on drugs and transportation. He said: “When I am governor, I will transfer these palliatives, these subsidies to my people. For instance, the doctors will not pay tax. For instance, the teachers will not pay tax. Those two groups will not pay tax. “Out of this N250 billion plus, I will transfer it into cards, whereby for those that cannot pay N50,000 per year in tax, I will create a card that you can pay N10,000 per year in tax, but you will get a subsidy in your drugs and you will get a subsidy in your transportation. This is giving money back to the people of Lagos State because I have it. Mr President has given it to me and I am giving it to you.” The PDP candidate also promised free education, saying the funds available to the state would enable him to implement the policy. Justifying the proposed tax exemption for doctors, he said: “We need close to about 15,000 doctors in Lagos State as we speak, but right now we have only about 3,000. So, if 3,000 doctors are not paying tax, please give me a break.” He described teachers as critical to the state’s future, arguing that they must receive proper training and support to prepare children for leadership and professional responsibilities. Doherty further condemned attacks on political activities and disclosed that some people he described as area boys had pulled down his campaign posters around Oregun and the Third Mainland Bridge. He said his Director-General had reported the incident to the police, adding that he would visit the Department of State Services, DSS. items.title: Flour gets costlier as imports stay insufficient
items.description: KARACHI: Amid a persistent shortfall, the arrival of imported wheat has so far failed to bring any relief to consumers, as wheat and wheat flour prices continue to rise. Retailers jacked up the rates of flour No. 2.5 and fine flour to Rs180 and Rs200 per kg, up by Rs10 per kg, citing an increase in the rates by the millers. So far, more than 100,000 tonnes of wheat have arrived in the country since the last week of October. Initially, the rate of wheat had plunged to Rs130 from Rs140 per kg after the arrival of the first ship carrying 51,000 tonnes on Oct 28. The open market, however, saw grain prices reverting to Rs140 per kg last week, forcing millers to raise prices of different flour varieties. Cereal Association of Pakistan (CAP) Chairman Muzammil Chappal told Dawn that he had been urging the government since May about a possible shortage of four million tonnes this season and at least allowing the private sector to import 2m tonnes, but the government had not paid any heed. Stakeholders estimate 3-4 million tonnes shortage of wheat The country is facing a crisis despite a 4.3pc rise in wheat production to 29.61m tonnes in FY26 from 28.40m tonnes in the preceding year, according to the Economic Survey FY26. According to Mr Chappal, annual demand for wheat ranges between 31m and 32m tonnes. He said, irrespective of the official wheat harvest of over 29m tonnes in FY26, the government needs to realise that demand for grain is rising as the population grows by over 3pc every year. Rauf Ibrahim, a wholesaler and trader, said the country needs at least 3m tonnes of wheat, as the new crop from Sindh and Punjab will enter markets between March and May next year. He said the federal and provincial governments have not launched any effective campaign against hoarders and stock pilferers since the wheat crop hit the markets in FY26. He urged the government to check commodity stocks, especially wheat, in markets and godowns, as speculators and investors have been active in commodity investing. Mr Ibrahim said millers raised the price of flour No. 2.5, Maida and Fine Flour to Rs8,100, Rs9,000 and Rs9,150, respectively, from Rs7,800, Rs8 ,400 and Rs8,550 per 50kg bag. High quality Chakki flour is available at Rs200 per kg in the wholesale market, while retailers are charging Rs215. Millers had raised the prices of different varieties by Rs20 per kg, but later started reducing rates ahead of the arrival of imported wheat. However, they started giving price shocks to consumers again amid the absence of any vigil by the authorities. One of the reasons behind rising wheat prices in Karachi, Mr Ibrahim said, is that Sindh has been waiting for imported wheat. Millers are facing a dearth of grain in the open market as the arrival of the commodity from Punjab has stopped. A miller, who asked not to be named, said the situation was alarming as prices had shot up in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as well despite the arrival of imported wheat. The miller claimed there are no uniform flour rates of the entire mill community as every mill is issuing rates as per its wheat stocks and market situation. Imported quantity not sufficient He said imported wheat would prove highly insufficient. For example, he added, only Karachi mills require 80,000 bags of 100kg daily for wheat grinding. Mr Ibrahim said the federal and provincial governments had yet to wake up over the shortage, which is hurting the low- and middle-income groups hard. “They will shudder at the thought of paying Rs2,000 for a 10kg flour bag.” He urged the government to check the stocks of flour millers as they usually keep one to two months’ stocks of grain. Tandoor owners are in a fix as they confront two problems — high rates for both flour and LPG. So far they have kept the prices of Chapati, Naan, Sheermal/Taftaan and Qulcha unchanged at Rs20, Rs30-35, Rs100-110 and Rs90-100, respectively. Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

items.title: Cooking gas price rises 14% to N1,600/kg as shortage bites
items.description: …National supply inadequate to meet demand – NALPGAM ..Falcon CEO advocates infrastructure-focused subsidies By Udeme Akpan & Ediri Ejoh The price of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG), popularly known as cooking gas, has risen by 14 per cent to N1,600 per kilogramme (kg) in November 2026, from N1,400 in October, amid growing supply shortages. Checks by Vanguard yesterday showed that several suppliers had run out of commercial stocks in Lagos and other parts of the country, with Dangote Petroleum Refinery among the few suppliers with available products. The development has sustained the upward movement in cooking gas prices over the past three months, raising concerns about the adequacy of domestic supply to meet growing demand. National supply inadequate to meet demand — NALPGAM Speaking with Energy Vanguard, National President of the Nigerian Association of Liquefied Petroleum Gas Marketers (NALPGAM), Mr. Inyang Edu, said the scarcity exposed the gap between national supply figures and the actual experience of consumers. He said: “The national supply is still struggling to keep pace with actual consumption. Although domestic LPG supply has increased, demand has also grown. “If this imbalance persists, the market must draw on existing inventories or secure additional supplies to maintain availability. A rise in supply is not sufficient to stabilise prices if consumption continues to exceed incoming volumes.” Edu identified inadequate storage and transportation infrastructure as additional constraints, explaining that the availability of gas at production facilities or coastal terminals did not guarantee access in inland markets. “The cost of transporting LPG over long distances, road conditions, haulage charges, loading and offloading, storage limitations and the availability of suitable LPG trucks can all contribute to regional price differences,” he said. He warned that increased national production should not be mistaken for improved supply across all states, particularly those far from major supply points. He added: “The appropriate policy is therefore not to eliminate imports indiscriminately, but to use domestic production as the foundation of supply while retaining sufficient flexibility to cover genuine shortfalls.” Falcon CEO advocates infra structure-focused subsidies Similarly, Chief Executive Officer of Falcon Corporation Limited, Audrey Joe-Ezigbo, has called for subsidies to target infrastructure that reduces LPG delivery costs rather than the price of the product. Speaking during a panel session on government-led LPG interventions at the 16th NLCGA Conference and Exhibition in Abuja, she stressed the need for coordinated government and private-sector investment to sustain household adoption. “We should subsidise access, not consumption. That means funding the infrastructure that lowers delivery costs, such as inland depots, bottling plants and better logistics, rather than the price. Some of these incentives already exist, and we need more of them,” she said. Joe-Ezigbo noted that transportation costs significantly affect what consumers in northern Nigeria pay for cooking gas, adding that trucking, railways and pipelines would be critical to expanding nationwide distribution. “We should avoid subsidising the molecule itself, because that discourages the investment needed to expand LPG use,” she said. She also called for improved household purchasing power and greater awareness of LPG’s health benefits, particularly as an alternative to traditional cooking fuels. On measuring the success of government interventions, she recommended tracking whether households benefiting from support programmes could independently afford cylinder refills at prevailing market prices 24 to 36 months after the assistance ended. To attract private investment, she advocated guaranteed supply, predictable regulations and an enforceable domestic LPG supply obligation, backed by performance-based offtake contracts linked to verified refills. items.title: Abia approves ₦1.04bn for SMEs, reviews ASEPA workers’ pay
items.description: …₦382.9m disbursed to 31 businesses By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — Abia State Government has secured approval for ₦1.041 billion in intervention funding for small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs), in a move aimed at expanding businesses, stimulating job creation and improving access to affordable credit. Of the amount, ₦382.9 million has already been disbursed to 29 micro-enterprises and two small and medium-scale businesses, while another ₦206.7 million in approved applications is undergoing documentation ahead of disbursement. The state government also announced a review of the remuneration of ad-hoc workers engaged by the Abia State Environmental Protection Agency (ASEPA), with the new payment structure taking effect from November 2026. Commissioner for Information, Prince Okey Kanu, who disclosed the developments during the weekly briefing on the State Executive Council meeting at Government House, Umuahia, said the SME intervention was being implemented through the Bank of Industry (BOI). Kanu, represented by the Special Adviser to the Governor on Media and Publicity, Mr Fredinald Ekeoma, said the initiative was part of Governor Alex Otti’s administration’s efforts to strengthen the state’s productive sector and create sustainable employment opportunities. Providing further details, Commissioner for Industries and SMEs, Mazi Mike Akpara, said the outstanding approved facilities would be released once beneficiaries fulfilled the necessary conditions, including documentation and provision of guarantors and collateral, where applicable. He stressed that access to the intervention was not restricted by political affiliation, insisting that any genuine business operating in Abia was eligible. “Whether you belong to the Labour Party, PDP or APC, we are not concerned about that. Once you are doing business in Abia and can provide evidence of your business operations, you are eligible to benefit. “SMEs are the engine of the economy, and this initiative is intended to encourage and strengthen them,” Akpara said. He said interested businesses could access the programme through the Ministry of Industries and SMEs at the Nnamdi Azikiwe Secretariat, Umuahia, or the BOI office in Aba. Akpara described the facility as a major relief for local entrepreneurs, given its relatively low interest rates of 8.5 per cent for overdrafts and 7.5 per cent for other facilities, with a three-year repayment period. He contrasted the rates with commercial bank lending rates, which he said could rise to between 28 and 30 per cent, arguing that the intervention would ease the financing burden on businesses and improve their capacity to expand. In another development, Kanu said the Ministry of Industries and SMEs had verified and documented more than 110 workshops and 120 shops at the Ohiya-Umuogo-Nsukwe Industrial Cluster. He said the exercise aligned with Goal Eight of the Sustainable Development Goals, which focuses on inclusive economic growth, productive employment and decent work. On the forthcoming AfrICANDO 2026 conference, the Information Commissioner announced that Governor Otti would formally declare the global event open on Tuesday, November 17, at the International Conference Centre, Umuahia. He said the conference would attract local and international participants, offering opportunities for investment partnerships, trade expansion and business development across different sectors. Kanu urged the media to give the event adequate coverage, noting that Abia was open to investors seeking viable business opportunities. The Commissioner also dismissed any suggestion that ongoing political activities ahead of the 2027 general elections had slowed down governance in the state. He said the machinery of government remained fully operational despite the distractions associated with electioneering, adding that preparations for the 2027 fiscal year were nearing completion. “In this connection, we affirm that the Abia State 2027 Budget is almost ready for presentation to the Abia State House of Assembly,” he said. items.title: Dry season farming: Shettima directs swift release of 3m fertiliser bags nationwide
items.description: ‎—Orders ONSA to monitor declared stocks ahead of distribution ‎ ‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ‎ ‎ABUJA — THE Vice President Senator Kashim Shettima has directed relevant government agencies and stakeholders in the fertiliser industry to expedite arrangements for the production and release of over three million bags of fertiliser to farmers across the country ahead of the forthcoming dry-season farming. ‎ ‎The directive followed President Bola Tinubu’s approval of funding under the Renewed Hope Agricultural Stabilisation and Productivity Initiative, aimed at making fertiliser more affordable, boosting food production and reviving Nigeria’s fertiliser blending industry. ‎ ‎The Vice President gave the directive on Monday at the Presidential Villa during a meeting with stakeholders in the fertiliser sector in Abuja, where the Fertiliser Producers and Suppliers Association of Nigeria (FEPSAN) disclosed that available raw materials could support the production of approximately three million bags of NPK fertiliser within the next few weeks. ‎ ‎He also directed the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) to verify and track fertiliser stocks declared by stakeholders to ensure transparency, accountability and a hitch-free distribution exercise. ‎ ‎He further urged the NSA’s office to ensure that farming communities in states facing security challenges are not neglected in the distribution programme, stressing the need for the intervention to reach farmers in vulnerable and hard-to-access areas. ‎ ‎Speaking on the broader economic importance of the presidential intervention, the Vice President said revitalising Nigeria’s fertiliser industry would strengthen agricultural productivity while creating jobs and supporting rural livelihoods. ‎ ‎”A strong fertilizer value chain supports hundreds of thousands of direct and indirect jobs. Revitalizing this sector is therefore important not only for agriculture but also for employment, rural livelihoods and economic activities across the country,” he stated. ‎ ‎Senator Shettima expressed concern that many of the country’s fertiliser blending plants were operating below capacity despite the growing demand for affordable agricultural inputs. ‎ ‎”Today, many of our fertilizer blending plants are operating below capacity at the same time the high cost of fertilizer continues to increase the cost of production for our farmers,” he observed. ‎ ‎According to him, President Tinubu’s intervention is designed to address these challenges by stimulating domestic production, restoring jobs and making fertiliser available to farmers at affordable prices. ‎ ‎”The government wants to support the rehabilitation and full utilization of our fertilizer blending capacity. We want the factories producing, we want workers back to work. We want transporters, warehouse, and agro-dealers to be engaged again,” he said. ‎ ‎The Vice President emphasised that farmers remained the principal beneficiaries of the initiative, noting that the Federal Government would purchase fertiliser produced by Nigerian blending companies and make it available at affordable prices. ‎ ‎”But ultimately the Nigerian farmer is at the centre of this initiative. Under the Renewed Hope Agricultural Stabilisation and Productivity Initiative, government intends to purchase fertilizers produced by Nigerian blenders and make it available to our farmers at affordable prices,” he added. ‎ ‎Senator Shettima thanked industry operators and other stakeholders for their willingness to partner with the government, stressing that the success of the intervention would depend on timely production, effective coordination and efficient distribution. ‎ ‎”Every stakeholder is expected to prepare accordingly in ensuring the success of the Presidential mandate to deliver fertilizer to farmers for the fast approaching dry-season farming,” he charged. ‎ ‎Earlier, the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Senator Abubakar Atiku Bagudu, said President Tinubu’s directive was aimed at making agricultural inputs more affordable while strengthening domestic production and food security. ‎ ‎He disclosed that stakeholders had identified approximately 496,000 metric tonnes of fertiliser-related stocks, describing the quantity as a reasonable starting point for implementing the programme. ‎ ‎”From what has been presented, we have about 496,000 metric tonnes of stock, and it is a good, reasonable starting point,” the minister said. ‎ ‎Bagudu assured that the government would work with relevant stakeholders to identify additional funding opportunities through existing programmes to sustain the intervention beyond the immediate presidential directive. ‎ ‎”We will work with every other stakeholder to identify other government programmes that will have funding that can be used to support this initiative even beyond the duration of the President’s directive,” he stated. ‎ ‎Also speaking, the President of FEPSAN, Alhaji Abubakar Sadiq Kassim, commended President Tinubu for personally intervening to revive the country’s fertiliser industry. ‎ ‎”I want to thank the President for taking a personal interest in reviving the Nigerian fertiliser industry. We are extremely encouraged by this intervention because this is about food security, jobs, rural livelihoods and economic and social stability of our country,” he said. ‎ ‎Kassim noted that Nigeria had already made substantial investments in fertiliser blending plants, warehouses, distribution infrastructure and agro-dealer networks, but many of these facilities were operating below their installed capacity. ‎ ‎He explained that reviving the industry would not only increase fertiliser availability but also restore economic activities across production, transportation, storage and distribution networks. ‎ ‎According to him, FEPSAN members had completed an assessment of available NPK fertiliser stocks, raw materials and the industry’s capacity to produce additional quantities within the implementation period. ‎ ‎”Based on information received from our members, the raw materials currently available can support the production of about 148,000 metric tonnes of NPK 20-10-10 within the next few weeks as targeted. This will give about three million bags of fertiliser,” he disclosed. ‎ ‎The FEPSAN president further revealed that members were holding approximately 29,000 metric tonnes of finished NPK fertiliser that could be immediately purchased and released for distribution. ‎ ‎He expressed confidence that the industry had the capacity to make approximately 3.5 million bags of fertiliser available within the stipulated period, noting that existing stocks and blending facilities were spread across different parts of the country. ‎ ‎Kassim added that the geographical distribution of the facilities would support faster delivery and reduce the logistical burden of reaching farmers. ‎ ‎As part of the implementation framework, President Tinubu also approved the Bank of Agriculture (BOA) and the Bank of Industry (BOI) to serve as fund administrators and financial intermediaries for the initiative. ‎ ‎In a related presentation, a representative of the Ministry of Finance Incorporated (MOFI) disclosed that the organisation had approximately 90,000 metric tonnes of materials on the ground, with additional goods in transit bringing the combined quantity to about 248,000 metric tonnes. items.title: Wike to opposition: Stop creating chaos to blame Tinubu
items.description: Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Mr Nyesom Wike, yesterday, accused opposition political parties of deliberately fomenting trouble to make it appear that President Bola Tinubu is responsible for political violence ahead of the 2027 elections. Wike made the allegation during the inauguration of the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council (APC-PCC) in the FCT at the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre in Abuja. The minister, who expressed confidence in the APC’s chances in the upcoming elections, claimed that opposition parties knew they had already lost and were creating political tension to discredit the ruling party. Wike said: “You have what it takes to win this election. The other parties know. Let me just tell you the simple truth. The other parties know they have lost the election. “What are they doing now? What they are doing now is to foment crisis—foment problems to make it look as if it is the government; it is the presidential candidate of the APC party who is fomenting trouble. “They (opposition) are the ones causing trouble. You (APC PCC) don’t need to cause trouble because you have already won the election. “They (opposition parties) foment trouble and report as if they are not the ones that have created that problem. So, we must be on alert.” Wike also told members of the Rainbow Coalition to make sure the African Democratic Congress, ADC, and the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, do not get 25 per cent of the votes in the FCT in the January 16, 2027 general elections. He warned the members against assuming the contest was already won, saying the election was a chance for the APC to show its political strength in the territory. On how to sell the president’s record, he said: “You don’t need to go and see a prophet. You don’t need to go and see any doctor or anybody to tell you what to do. It is obvious; it is factual. Look at what Mr President has done for the people of the FCT. These are the tools you need to campaign.” Wike also dared opposition politicians to set projects built before 2023 beside those delivered since Tinubu took office, arguing that the work going on in the city centre and the satellite towns spoke for itself. items.title: Punjab govt plans anti-rape legislation, speedy courts
items.description: LAHORE: The Punjab government on Monday announced plans to introduce an anti-rape law and set up “fast-track courts” to ensure speedy trials of cases involving violence against women and children, with a clear timeframe for their disposal. The decision was taken at a meeting chaired by Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz to review measures for the protection of women and children and improve the criminal justice system. “Women and children are among the most vulnerable segments of society and their protection remains a priority. Spec­ialised investigations are essential to securing convictions, while encouraging victims to report offe­nces is equally important to ensuring justice,” she said. While a special legal framework, the Anti-Rape (Investigation and Trial) Act, 2021, exists at the federal level for the expeditious investigation and trial of rape and sexual abuse cases involving women and children, it is yet to be seen if the provincial legislature adopts provisions of the same legislation or brings one tailored to the needs of Punjab. At the meeting, the chief minister stressed the need for effective legislation and stronger investigations to ensure that perpetrators did not escape punishment. Expressing concern over the low conviction rate in cases involving violence against women and children, she directed the police to enhance their investigative capabilities and strengthen preventive measures against such offences. It was agreed artificial intelligence be utilised to improve the quality of investigations and prosecution, besides ensuring the effective collection and preservation of audio and video evidence in cases involving women and children. According to a briefing by Inspector General of Police Rao Abdul Karim, around 1.24 million complaints concerning women had been registered at police stations across Punjab, with action completed in 92 per cent of the cases. The Women Virtual Police Station had also received nearly 125,000 complaints. The meeting was informed that more than 70,000 missing or abducted children had been recovered through the Virtual Centre for Child Safety, while 4,000 children with special needs had been reunited with their families during her tenure as chief minister of Punjab. Also, the authorities had solved 7,588 cases of child sexual abuse, according to the briefing. However, a particularly concerning finding was that people known to victims were involved in 71 per cent of reported sexual abuse cases involving women and children, underscoring the need for greater public awareness and preventive measures. At this, the chief minister called for a broader public awareness campaign to prevent violence against women and children and directed the relevant authorities to ensure professional investigations and effective prosecution so that those responsible were brought to justice. Published in Dawn, November 17th, 2026

items.title: 796 Afghans arrested in first week of November
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Law-en­forcement agencies arres­ted 796 Afghan nationals during the first week of November from Balochis­tan, Khyber Pakhtun­kh­­wa, Punjab and Islamabad. According to the latest update released jointly by UNHCR and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, out of all arrests and detentions, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders and undocumented Afghans represented 99 per cent of the total rate of arrest and detentions, and Proof of Registration (PoR) holders represent one per cent. Most of the arrests took place in Balochistan, follo­wed by Khyber-Pakht­u­n­khwa, Punjab and Islamabad. Across the country, the top three districts for arrest and detention this year were Chaghi, Peshawar and Karachi, the update says. Key findings of the report show cumulatively, from September 15 2023 to November 7 this year, 2,758,958 individuals have returned to Afghanistan. During the first week of November, the number of returns decreased by 16 per cent and deportation by 19 per cent, compared to the previous week of October. During the first week of this month, a total of 4,662 returns were reported, including 809 deportations. The decrease in returns and deportations reflects a fluctuation from the higher levels recorded in the previous week, while measures affecting Afghan nationals without valid visas remained in place. Among those who retur­ned between November 1 and 7, most were undocumented (78 per cent) followed by PoR holders (12pc) and ACC holders (10pc). Majority of the PoR retur­­ns were processed by UNHCR through the Vol­untary Repatriation Cent­res. Among those who were deported between Nov­­ember 1 and 7, most were undocumented (98pc) followed by PoR holders (1pc). Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

items.title: 2027: APC rallies deepening Nigerians’ anger, Kawu warns party leaders
items.description: …Senator decries disconnect between northern masses and political elite, urges grassroots mobilisation By Henry Umoru ABUJA — Chairman of the Senate Committee on Petroleum (Downstream), Senator Kawu Sumaila Suleiman (APC, Kano South), has warned the leadership of the All Progressives Congress (APC) that displays of opulence, celebrations and merrymaking at presidential campaign rallies are deepening the pains and anger of Nigerians. The senator, who is the APC senatorial candidate for the January 16, 2027 election, said there was a growing disconnect and misunderstanding between ordinary people in the North and the political elite. In a statement addressed to party leaders and members on Monday, his second intervention on the matter, Suleiman called for a change in the party’s approach and strategy ahead of the 2027 general elections. He urged the APC leadership and Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) to prioritise effective communication of President Bola Tinubu’s policies and ongoing reforms to Nigerians at the grassroots. The lawmaker also called on the party to identify and empower credible individuals and stakeholders with genuine grassroots influence in their respective constituencies rather than relying on what he described as “Abuja politicians” and entitled individuals disconnected from the people. In the statement titled, “A Clarion Call for Self-Reflection, Humility, and Grassroots Reconnection”, Suleiman said the party’s message was still not reaching ordinary Nigerians. He said: “Following my earlier message, we must once again be completely honest with ourselves: our message is still not reaching the grassroots. We need to acknowledge and accept that there is a growing disconnect and misunderstanding between the common people in the North and the political elites. We must change our approach and strategy. “There is an urgent need to effectively communicate our government’s policies and the ongoing reforms of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu directly to the grassroots.” The senator warned that the celebratory atmosphere at campaign rallies was insensitive to the hardship and insecurity confronting many Nigerians, particularly in the North. He urged party leaders to remember victims of terrorism, thousands of Nigerians displaced from their communities and those forced to flee across the border into the Niger Republic. “The current displays of celebration, opulence, and pomp-dancing and merrymaking during presidential campaign rallies are only deepening the pains and anger of the citizens. “We must remember the countless people currently trapped in the hands of terrorists, the thousands suffering in internally displaced persons (IDP) camps, and those who have been forced to flee across the border into the Niger Republic,” he said. Suleiman called for deep reflection among APC leaders, reminding them of the responsibility entrusted to them by Tinubu. “It is time for deep self-reflection. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has entrusted us with a sacred responsibility (Amana), and we must protect and honour it,” he said. Acknowledging that his message might offend some party leaders, the senator said genuine loyalty required speaking honestly about issues affecting the party’s collective interest. He also cautioned against sycophancy and selfish political ambitions, urging party members to place the country’s stability and the party’s success above personal interests. Suleiman prayed for Tinubu’s continued success, victory for APC candidates in the forthcoming elections and lasting peace and security across Nigeria. The post 2027: APC rallies deepening Nigerians’ anger, Kawu warns party leaders appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: COP31 chief urges climate finance action, highlights China's role
items.description: As the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference ( COP31 ) entered its final week on Monday, COP31 President Murat Kurum urged countries to deliver on existing finance pledges. Kurum, also Türkiye's environment, urbanization and climate change minister, said in Antalya that fulfilling existing commitments is key to advancing climate action. He highlighted the climate finance decision taken in Baku to mobilize $300 billion annually by 2035 under the 2024 UN deal channeling funds to developing nations. To help translate financing commitments into concrete action, Türkiye is rolling out the Climate Implementation Bridge mechanism in partnership with the UN Development Programme (UNDP), Kurum said. On China's role in the COP31 process, Kurum said China has work underway on almost every topic within the conference's action agenda and goals. "China is very good in renewable energy, and I can say it leads the world on this issue," he said. He also highlighted China's technology and know-how, as well as its willingness to share them "with full transparency," noting that renewable energy investments are steadily rising while costs in the sector continue to fall. As the two-week conference heads toward its conclusion on Friday, the minister said Türkiye seeks outcomes in Antalya across adaptation, mitigation and climate finance, with countries expected to track the decisions taken, monitor the results and hold themselves accountable for the steps ahead.

items.title: Vers l'élargissement du service du Roaming national sans changement de tarif
items.description: Le gouvernement prévoit d'élargir le service du Roaming national qui permet aux abonnés des services de téléphonie mobile l'utilisation du réseau d'un autre opérateur sans changement de tarif, avec la transition automatique entre les réseaux, a indiqué, lundi, le ministre de l'Intelligence artificielle, de la Transition numérique et de la Réforme de l’administration, Ahmed Rahhou. En réponse à une question orale à la Chambre des représentants sur « la généralisation des services des opérateurs de télécom à l'ensemble du territoire national », Rahhou a expliqué que ce service couvre actuellement plus de 7.000 zones, notant que pour en bénéficier l'abonné devra changer de réseau, alors que le téléphone sera capable de chercher automatiquement le réseau disponible pour effectuer les appels, à l'instar du fonctionnement du Roaming à l'étranger. Le ministère œuvrera à obliger l'opérateur qui couvre à lui seul une zone d'ouvrir son réseau aux abonnés des autres opérateurs, a-t-il poursuivi, ajoutant que certaines zones ne permettent pas, sur le plan économique, la présence des trois opérateurs. S'agissant des zones difficiles d'être liées au réseau terrestre, il a précisé que son département examinera, avec le concours de l'Agence nationale de réglementation des télécommunications (ANRT) et en partenariat avec les opérateurs nationaux, la possibilité de bénéficier des services de nouveaux réseaux de satellites, tels que « Starlink » et « Kuiper », de façon sûre et sécurisée, pour couvrir les « zones blanches » qui ne disposent pas d'études de faisabilité économiques pour l'établissement de réseaux terrestres. Dans le même sens, Rahhou a fait savoir qu'un inventaire préliminaire du taux de couverture par les réseaux télécoms a été achevé, dans le cadre d'une opération de contrôle ayant concerné près de 50.000 km de route, notant que la couverture englobe actuellement 100% des routes nationales et régionales. La distance restante, estimée à 15.700 km, se compose de routes provinciales dont le contrôle se poursuivra en 2027, a-t-il dit, ajoutant que le ministère veillera à leur couverture par les opérateurs lors de l'année prochaine ou dans deux ans au plus tard. Pour ce qui est du monde rural, Rahhou a souligné la poursuite des efforts pour l'amélioration de la couverture internet, par le biais du Plan national du haut et du très haut débit, dont la deuxième phase permettra la couverture de 2.000 zones rurales ayant une couverture faible ou inexistante au cours de cette année. Il a de même indiqué que la liste des zones concernées sera révisée selon une approche participative impliquant les différents intervenants, dont les parlementaires, les autorités locales et instances élues, et après des visites de terrain, avec la possibilité de réorganiser les priorités aux niveaux des points programmés. The post Vers l'élargissement du service du Roaming national sans changement de tarif appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Why Warnock Didn’t Sleep on Mississippi
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts “I am here because I am tired of the South being overlooked or diminished in terms of its electoral importance,” Senator Raphael Warnock told Mississippi Today back in October after stumping for Scott Colom. A month later, Colom won. He’s the first Black Mississippian elected to the U.S. Senate since Reconstruction. “We lose elections by the margins of our disengagement,” Warnock said then. “Mississippi is a blue state; it just doesn’t know it yet.” Warnock, the pastor of Atlanta’s Ebenezer Baptist Church, was one of the few national Democrats who spent time in Mississippi this cycle. He raised hundreds of thousands of campaign dollars. Last week, when news outlets finally called the race in Mississippi, America woke up to the race everyone was “sleeping on,” as Warnock put it back in April. Democrats, who had ceded the South to Republicans for the past several decades, now believe that the political possibilities in the region are changing and have even further to go; few Democrats on the national stage believe that as much as Warnock. For this week’s episode of Radio Atlantic , I spoke with Warnock at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta about the uptick in turnout in the 2026 midterms, how to protect the vote in future elections, and what his agenda looks like in the years to come. The following is a transcript of the episode: Senator Raphael Warnock: You have to compromise in politics. But I’m not going to compromise my integrity, just to maintain an office. [ Music ] Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic . I’m Adam Harris, and today: a conversation with Senator Raphael Warnock about voting rights, the South, and what he wants to get done in the next Congress. On January 5, 2021, Warnock became the first Black senator in Georgia’s history. A day later, rioters stormed the U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C. And to Warnock, both events represent America. Those dates—January 5 and January 6—represent the promise and the violence of its history And to him, when Scott Colom was declared the winner in Mississippi’s Senate race, Warnock believed it was another promising moment. Few people – including national Democrats – believed Colom’s win was possible, but Warnock did. He was one of the few who supported him early and often. He says it’s because he believes a new South is a real possibility. On Thursday evening, at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, I sat down with Senator Warnock to talk about what needs to be done to protect voting rights, what political success looks like for Democrats, and how to hold the tension that America is both January 5 and January 6. Here’s our conversation: Adam Harris: Senator, it’s great to be with you this evening. Raphael Warnock: It’s great to be home. I just landed a few minutes ago. I came straight here. Didn’t pass go, didn’t collect $200. Harris: I love it. Warnock: Good to see everybody. Harris: Yeah, absolutely, and thank you all for joining us. I’ve been looking forward to this conversation, particularly as we’ve seen the South change a bit over the last couple of days. For a long time, political possibility in the South has been sort of limited by both discrimination and also sort of lack of imagination. In 2021, you became Georgia’s first Black senator. What does Scott Colom’s win in Mississippi, what do these wins in Georgia tell us about political possibility in the South? Warnock: What a remarkable moment in American history. And I’m just honored and deeply humbled to be a small part of it. I’m so happy for the people of Mississippi. But let’s be clear: Mississippi did an incredible thing for the whole country. The country is better. They nudged us a little closer to our ideals. And Scott Colom ran an incredibly innovative, creative, and scrappy campaign because he had very little resources. People didn’t believe. But I wanna be clear, because sometimes on the other side of these victories, we forget what it costs. This didn’t roll in on the wheels of inevitability. I know what it’s like for people to believe, for people to think you can’t do it. And it always looks impossible until it’s done. That’s where we were here in Georgia. Cycle after cycle, we kept telling folks, It can happen in Georgia , and they didn’t believe us. Harris: You just invest. Warnock: And we kept falling short. Don’t forget that. Because it’s easy to forget now that I’m here. And the great Jon Ossoff is here. A Black senator and a Jewish senator in one fell swoop. Right? But representing the whole state. But I don’t want you to miss this: The people of Mississippi did an amazing thing. I know you were wondering, Well, when are they gonna finish counting all those ballots? But here’s the question you ought to ask yourself: Why is that the case? So there were provisional ballots, and why were there provisional ballots? Because people had been purged from the roll. Georgia, by the way, was quite good at that. They purged 500,000 voters one Saturday night here in Georgia. And so people’s names had been purged from the rolls, and so that’s why they had to cast a provisional ballot. And they had to vote on Election Day—only on Tuesday, because you don’t vote early in Mississippi without an excuse. So think about that. Why do you need an excuse to vote? So early voting is virtually nonexistent. You’ve got these rural communities where it’s not necessarily easy to get to the polls. It’s a poll tax on working people because the only time you can vote is on Tuesday during work hours. And somehow those folks overcame all of those barriers just to be able to exercise the franchise, which is not a privilege. Don’t ever say voting is a privilege. It’s not a privilege; it’s a right. It’s a right. Driving is a privilege. Voting is a right. And they overcame all of that, and here we are. Harris: And actually, to that point, speaking of the things that they overcame: One of the stories of this cycle was the turnout. Here in Georgia, you had 160,000 more Black folks cast ballots than cast ballots in 2022, right? But over the last two decades, we’ve seen voting protections weakened, right? This was done in spite of all of the ways that the franchise has been limited. And because voting is so foundational, as they said in 1886—the Supreme Court said that it was protective of all other rights, that voting was foundational to democracy. What does strengthening that right to vote look like? Warnock: Well, it’s job one, and I spend a lot of time working on voting rights and strengthening our democracy. Because voting rights is not just one other issue alongside other issues. This radical idea that no matter your income, no matter your race, no matter who you are, you get to vote and your vote gets to count—that’s the framework in which we get to fight, so we have to always preserve that. And we have witnessed the erosion of those fundamental rights over the last few years. And so it’s important that you help your neighbors who say, “What do you mean? Everybody can vote.” You’re right. So the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendment were passed following slavery, part of the work of Reconstruction. So I want you to remember that Black people had a right to vote, at least on paper, for 100 years before the voting-rights law was passed. So just because it’s on paper, that doesn’t mean there aren’t real barriers. And Mississippi embodies that, but it’s not alone. So we have seen the erosion of voting rights over the last several years. That is part of the ugly legacy, in my view, of the Roberts Court, Shelby v. Holder , which said that the states that had previously been under what’s known as “preclearance”— We’re way past that. Why are we still doing that? And they removed those protections. Ruth Bader Ginsburg, bless her memory, when she wrote her dissenting opinion to that decision, she said, “We’re removing our umbrella in the middle of a rainstorm because we’re not getting wet.” And her words proved to be tragically correct. I don’t want it to get lost on you that in spite of these incredible turnouts that we’re seeing and the incredible results we saw last Tuesday in response to this attack on voting rights—in response to Callais , right? Which added fuel to partisan gerrymandering—Black and brown voters alongside white sisters and brothers created a coalition of conscience, responded in response to this. But it shouldn’t be lost that in the years since Shelby v. Holder , the racial voter-turnout gap has widened. And it’s widened twice as fast in the states that used to be under preclearance. The very states that have a history of discrimination, and so they’re under Section 5—which says that if you’re gonna make some changes, you gotta run it by the Justice Department—that gap has increased twice as fast in those states. So you’ve got Shelby v. Holder . You’ve got Citizens United , which is a scourge on our democracy. It’s diminishing the voices of ordinary people while raising the voices of corporate, wealthy, and well-connected entities. And then you had Callais in which the Supreme Court was deeply intellectually dishonest when it said you can’t have minority opportunity districts because that’s reverse racism, while leaving partisan gerrymandering intact. And we know that especially in the South, you can’t neatly disaggregate partisan gerrymandering from racial gerrymandering. I think race was the reason why we had it in the first place. And so we literally saw these states gerrymandering the districts while folks were voting. And so what happened last Tuesday is the American people stood up and said, Enough . They were upset about this. They’re crushed by these terrible gas prices, the price of groceries. And they stood up to take back their democracy. For me, I take it as a sacred trust. And I feel deeply obligated to try to deliver for the people who gave us a chance to fight for them. Harris: And when you think about that, delivering for the folks who fought, right? You argue in the book that looks like the John Lewis voting-rights— Warnock: What book are you talking about? Hold it up. ( Audience laughs .) Listen, I got a 10-year-old and a 7-year-old. I have college tuition to pay. You know, the Senate has been a place where the aristocracy has sent its sons, and then daughters. That is not my story. The Crooked Places Made Straight: Reflections on the Moral Meaning of America . Harris: So in the first couple chapters of the book, you focus on voting. You mentioned Citizens United . This was the most expensive midterm race in history: $12 billion spent in this midterm cycle. And that number seems to grow with every election. How do we begin to wean off of money in politics? Warnock: It’s insane, when I think about what it cost for me to win this Senate seat. Because all of us are part of that system. I’m embarrassed how much money it took for me to win this seat, but at the same time, I know I can’t unilaterally disarm. I wouldn’t be here. But Citizens United —one of the most important things we can do for our democracy is to get dark money out of our system, and to create a system where billionaires spend a whole lot less on elections and a whole lot more in taxes. The American people sense in their gut—because they’re smart; they get it—that the system is rigged. And they’re right. They’re not wrong about that. It’s rigged. But we’ve seen increasing wealth inequality in this country since Citizens United . That’s not an accident. The wealthy, the well-connected, the top 1 percent or so of the country that’s got more money than the bottom 53 percent, they like it like this. And that wealth inequality is greater than it was during the Gilded Age. And, so for me, it’s a democracy question. I want people to have a voice in the direction of their country and their place within it, which is why we’ve gotta pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act ( Audience applauds .) which would deal with dark money in our politics. We need to reverse Citizens United , even if we have to do it by a constitutional amendment. ( Audience applauds .) We need to get rid of partisan gerrymandering ( Audience applauds .) in our politics. Gerrymandering is turning the democracy on its head so that rather than the people picking their representatives, gerrymandering is the politicians cherry-picking their voters. So we need to deal with partisan gerrymandering, and we need to make sure that the so-called SAVE Act never sees the light of day. Harris: Do you think any of those legislative actions are possible in this next Congress? It’ll be a lame-duck session. But do you think any of that is possible in this Congress? Warnock: Well, one of the things—so I’d like to pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act because it’ll address a lot of these things that I’m talking about. But in the meantime, I would like to offer in the new Congress a slender and skinny bill to deal with gerrymandering. And I have that bill. I’m gonna offer that bill in the Congress. We ought to deal with gerrymandering. I’m a Democrat, but I’m an American first. And I think it’s bad for the democracy that there are so few truly competitive congressional districts in our country. And so folks got busy after Callais last spring, gerrymandering these districts a few months before the election. Well, as we say in church, God works in mysterious ways . And maybe, maybe after some of my Republican friends got crushed in their own gerrymandered districts, there might be some takers who will join me in this effort to get rid of gerrymandering altogether. [ Break ] Harris: You talk about that hope in your book, The Crooked Places Made Straight. Warnock: There it is. ( Audience laughs .) Harris: ( Laughs .) In your book, you look at politics through a moral lens, through a Christian lens. You talk about where your hope comes from, sort of through the Book of Isaiah in particular. And it’s easy to get cynical about politics. At one point, you wrote about the ways that your congregation at Ebenezer was worried that politics would make their pastor sort of lose his prophetic voice, that it would sort of change you. Can you talk about how your faith informs your politics, and how you can keep it central through the cynicism of the political arena? Warnock: I am not a senator who used to be a pastor. I’m a pastor who serves in the Senate, and my faith is what got me in this mess in the first place, called politics. I have a faith that seriously believes that faith ought to live in the messiness and complexity of everyday life. I’ve never wanted a stained-glass-window faith that’s encased in a museum, and you bump into it on Sunday morning, and then you walk out, and then you pick it back up on Sunday. My faith lives in the public square. Always has. Long before I served in the Senate, long before I knew I would even run. My whole career, I’ve been at Ebenezer now 21 years, and I pastored for many years before that. I’ve always been an activist pastor. I was fighting for health care before I was your senator. I was trying to get Georgia to expand Medicaid way back in 2014, when the ACA was passed. I was trying to get our state to expand Medicaid. What drives me to your question is: I remain rooted in my faith. I return to my pulpit every Sunday morning. I still serve as pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, and folks ask me, “Why do you do that? Because you’re pretty busy as a senator.” Well, I return to my church, and I continue to lead that church, because I don’t wanna spend all my time talking to politicians. I’m afraid I might accidentally become one. I wanna be a public servant who’s in politics. You have to compromise in politics. But I’m not going to compromise my integrity, just to maintain an office. I’m grateful for this set of tools for the period of time that I have it, and whenever that changes, I’ll have another set of tools. But the mission is the same: human liberation; human thriving; building a country where every child has a chance, where a child’s outcome is not based on their parents’ income, where people have access to health care and affordable housing and the dignity that comes with that. Harris: You wrote in the book, “We all share a basic human longing for purpose and connection that transcends our narrow self-interest.” And that struck me, particularly given that there are folks who call themselves Christian at the moment who argue that empathy is something that their flocks should look away from. Can you talk about that idea that we share that longing for things beyond ourselves, when you have examples of folks who do not? Warnock: So one of the things that is unfortunate and keeps me up at night is the recognition that some of the meanest and most hateful voices in our country are Christian voices. The data shows that evangelical Christians—again, not all—but the data shows that evangelical Christians are more likely than any other group to blame the poor for their poverty, to somehow surmise that their material deficiency is somehow reflective of a moral deficiency. And so I want you to think about that. Like, what is it about our theology, what’s being preached on Sunday morning that causes people to blame poor people for being poor, and to moralize about that and not see this wealth inequality that I’m talking about, the fact that people work and they don’t have a livable wage. To me, when I see this mean-spirited Jesus, I don’t know who they’re talking about. The Jesus that whom I preach on Sunday morning—I’m a Matthew 25 Christian. Said, “I was hungry and you fed me. I was thirsty; you gave me something to drink. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison; you came to see about me. I was a stranger, an immigrant, and you welcomed me.” And they asked Jesus, “When were you hungry? When were you thirsty? When were you sick? When were you a prisoner? When were you an immigrant?” He said, “Inasmuch as you’ve done it unto the least of these, you’ve done it also unto me.” And so that’s my faith. I don’t know how anyone gets this idea that empathy somehow is anathema. Empathy is not only central to Christian faith; empathy is central to all of the great faith traditions. I think empathy is the first step of good public policy and good politics. If you can’t see your neighbor, how are you going to represent your neighbor? Harris: We’ve discussed voting. Where do you see other opportunities for action, for policy, change? Warnock: Well, the great thing is that the American people stood up, and they spoke very clearly. And they are sick and tired of this lawless war of choice that is making us less safe and driving up gas prices, the price of diesel. And when you drive up the price of diesel, because almost everything you got—everything you have arrived on a truck—so it’s raising the price of everything. They’re weary of these tariffs, which is a tax, a sales tax on everything you buy, and they want us to fix health care. So that’s what I wanna do. I wanna end the war. I wanna stop these tariffs. I wanna pass these premium tax credits so that people’s health-care premiums aren’t twice as much next year as they are now—triple, quadruple in some cases. And then once we stop the bleeding, I think we need to lay out a bold vision for our country. I still think we can do big things. And I’m not convinced that we suffer from a poverty of resources. We suffer from a poverty of moral imagination and moral courage. And so I’m ready to roll up my sleeves and work alongside all of my colleagues, Democrats and Republicans, and move the country forward. Harris: We’ve seen some of the ways that Republicans have sort of doubled down on the policy of the first two years of this administration, though, promoting Stephen Miller to become the chief of staff. Jim Jordan will be the House minority leader. What do you make of that doubling down? Is there space to work with the president? Do you think that the administration will be— Warnock: Listen, we have to do what the American people asked us to do. And we have to fight for this with or without our Republican colleagues. But we need some guardrails on this president. That’s a good first start. We literally witnessed a Congress that went along with everything he did. Watching the last two years, you wouldn’t know that tariffs are in the purview and authority of Congress. I know you forgot because the Congress isn’t asserting its authority. What we’ve witnessed in tragic fashion is what happens if one branch voluntarily just hands over its power. I’ll tell you what happens: You get Pete Hegseth as the secretary of defense; and you get Robert F. Kennedy as the secretary of health and human services, and all of a sudden you’re dealing with measles, again. Measles? Really? Harris: Measles. Warnock: It means that you’ve got tariffs on just about everything, and people are crushed. And thankfully, the American people, even in ruby-red districts who’ve been suffocating in this economy, said, Enough . And so we’ve got some guardrails on this president. When you get a result that you don’t want in an election, what you’re supposed to do is course-correct. Don’t start playing with the lines. What you’re supposed to do is course-correct. So hopefully with such a clear message, we can find some common ground to do things that the American people want us to do. Harris: You wrote that “America is both January 5 and January 6. It has always contained both of those elements throughout its history.” If this election is a January 5, how do we prevent the next January 6? Warnock: That’s a great question. On January 5, 2021, the people of Georgia did an amazing thing: They sent a kid who grew up in public housing—Cayton Homes Housing Project, Savannah, Georgia. First college graduate in my family, number 11 out of 12. My folks read the scriptures, “Be fruitful and multiply.” ( Audience laughs .) They sent this Black kid who grew up in the projects alongside a Jewish kid who was the son of an immigrant—both of us touched in different ways by John Lewis—to the United States Senate in one fell swoop, at a moment when we’re all suffocating under the thick air of COVID and the bigotry unleashed in the Trump years. And I was feeling great the next morning. I was like, Oh, I’ve arrived . I was on Morning Joe . I was on Good Morning America . I was on The View talking to Whoopi Goldberg. ( Audience laughs .) I had arrived. I was feeling really good about myself. That was the morning of January 6. And by lunchtime, we all know what happened. That other side of our grand American experiment reared its ugly head. And so January 5 is who we are, where a Black kid and a Jewish kid can be United States senators from Georgia. What we must hold in tension is the recognition that we’re both of those things. Both January 5 and January 6 tell us something important about who America is, and it’s too easy to say we’re one and not the other. When January 6 happened, people kept saying, This is not who we are . And I understand the sentiment that they were trying to express, but it’s not true. January 6 is who we are; it’s who we’ve always been. It’s a part of who we are, and when we’re in denial about that, we can’t fix it. The good news is that that’s not all that we are. We don’t have to ban books. We don’t have to lie about our history. We don’t have to pretend like our children are so tender and so fragile that we have to lie to them and call slavery a jobs program. I had an older father who was a World War II–era veteran. And it’s a blessing to have had an older father. There’s a wisdom that comes with that. And he used to tell us the story about how one day, while dressed in his soldier’s uniform, he had to give up his seat on the bus to a white teenager. He’s dressed in his soldier’s uniform, preparing to make the world safe for democracy. My old man is asked to give up his bus seat to a teenager because the skin he was wearing was apparently more important than the uniform he was wearing. And decades later, the man who had to give up his bus seat has a son who sits in a Senate seat. We’re both of those things. And what I love about the country is that we get to keep fighting for what’s the better part of that story. Because we don’t need to “make America great again.” This is a great country, and we’re just trying to push it a little bit closer to its ideals because it can be greater yet. ( Audience applauds .) Harris: Thank you so much. We’ll have to leave it there. [ Music ] This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Eibed is the executive producer of Podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues here at The Atlantic you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.
