items.title: Tunisie | Alerte au brouillard dense dès cette nuit
items.description: L'Institut national de la météorologie (INM) appelle à la vigilance en annonçant la formation d’un brouillard localement épais dès cette nuit, persistant jusqu’à la matinée du mardi 17 novembre. Dans un bulletin spécial publié dans la soirée de ce lundi 16 novembre 2026, les services météorologiques précisent que ce phénomène concernera principalement les régions côtières. La densité du brouillard sera particulièrement marquée dans les zones basses, aux abords du littoral ainsi que dans les environs des barrages et des zones forestières. Cette situation entraînera une baisse notable de la visibilité horizontale, qui pourrait chuter en dessous de 500 mètres par endroits, prévient l'INM. L'institut appelle ainsi les automobilistes et l'ensemble des usagers de la route à faire preuve de la plus grande prudence, notamment en réduisant leur vitesse et en maintenant les distances de sécurité. Une amélioration est attendue en cours de matinée, le brouillard devant commencer à se dissiper progressivement à partir de 9h. Y. N. items.title: Condamnation des administrateurs de Siguiri : le procureur de la Crief jubile, la défense conteste le verdict
items.description: Les réactions n’ont pas tardé après le verdict rendu dans l’affaire de l’orpaillage clandestin à Siguiri. Alors que les avocats des 22 anciens administrateurs territoriaux, condamnés à deux ans d’emprisonnement et à une amende individuelle de 10 millions de francs guinéens, envisagent d’éventuelles voies de recours, le procureur spécial de la CRIEF, Alphonse Charles Wright, s’est déclaré satisfait de la décision de la chambre de jugement. Condamnés pour complicité de dégradation de l’environnement, de destructions diverses et de pollution des eaux, les anciens administrateurs ne comptent visiblement pas en rester là. Leur avocat, Me Abdourahmane Dabo, a exprimé sa déception, tout en estimant que les arguments de la défense avaient été largement pris en compte par les juges. « Nous prenons la parole avec le cœur très serré parce que nous estimons que nous avons été entendus en grande partie mais, hélas, les juges composant cette chambre ont décidé de rentrer en condamnation contre nos clients », a-t-il déclaré. L’avocat a toutefois indiqué que la défense entendait d’abord se concerter avec les personnes condamnées avant de se prononcer sur la suite de la procédure. « Les voies de recours s’ouvrent aux parties. Nous allons essayer de voir. Si nécessaire, nous allons aviser », a-t-il ajouté. À l’inverse, le procureur spécial de la CRIEF, Alphonse Charles Wright, a salué le verdict, estimant que la responsabilité pénale des prévenus avait été établie. Il s’est notamment félicité de la condamnation des ressortissants étrangers impliqués dans l’exploitation minière illégale, mais aussi de celle des administrateurs territoriaux, dont la responsabilité a été retenue à titre subsidiaire. « Le ministère public est très satisfait puisque c'est à bon droit que la responsabilité pénale des personnes de sujets étrangers a été retenue, mais de façon subsidiaire, celle des administrateurs territoriaux », a affirmé le procureur spécial. Pour Alphonse Charles Wright, l’essentiel n’est pas tant la durée des peines prononcées que la reconnaissance judiciaire des faits reprochés aux prévenus. « Ce n'est pas le quantum de la peine qui nous importe. On pouvait même les condamner à un an […] Le plus important aujourd'hui, derrière cette décision, c'est que ce qui a été porté contre eux a été établi devant une juridiction indépendante », a-t-il insisté. Le procureur spécial considère également cette décision comme un avertissement à l’endroit des acteurs de l’exploitation minière clandestine. Il a rappelé, dans ce sens, que la protection de l’environnement demeure un enjeu majeur auquel les autorités judiciaires entendent accorder une attention particulière. Ainsi, au lendemain des condamnations prononcées par le juge Alpha Camara, les positions restent divergentes entre les parties. La défense se réserve la possibilité de faire appel après concertation avec ses clients, tandis que le ministère public entend, lui aussi, apprécier l’opportunité d’un éventuel recours.

items.title: Amantia Chief urges prioritisation of rural development to combat poverty and social vices
items.description: Newly enstooled Chief of Amantia in the Asante Akyem South District, Nana Kwadwo Bredu III, has expressed concern over the neglect of rural development by successive governments. H says the utter disregard for rural communities has left many of them without essential social amenities and economic opportunities, despite contributing to taxes for expected development. He has called on the government to prioritise development in rural communities as part of efforts to tackle poverty, unemployment and social vices among the youth. According to him, the lack of basic infrastructure and essential services in rural areas has contributed to poverty and exposed some young people to drug abuse and other social vices. Speaking at his official unveiling as the new chief of Amantia, Nana Kwadwo Bredu III bemoaned the inadequate provision of essential facilities, including quality schools, healthcare centres, accessible roads and potable drinking water in his community. He attributed these challenges to what he described as the government’s failure to give rural communities the needed development attention. “Before I became the chief of this community, there were several challenges relating to social amenities. I used my personal resources to address some of these problems, but we still need government intervention to bring further development to the community,” he said. Nana Kwadwo Bredu III also appealed to the youth to rally behind his leadership and contribute meaningfully towards the development of Amantia. “The youth are the future of this community and the country as a whole. I therefore urge you to support me through hard work, commitment and determination to build a better Amantia,” he stated. Meanwhile, the Queen Mother of Amantia has cautioned individuals and those falsely claiming the title of Amantia chief to desist from such actions. Some residents who attended the ceremony were delighted over the installation, describing it as a positive development for the community. They pledged their full support for the new chief, citing his contributions to community development even before his enstoolment. According to them, Nana Kwadwo Bredu III had demonstrated commitment to improving the community and deserved their collective support to achieve greater development. The ceremony saw residents dressed in red and displaying red banners as a symbol of their solidarity and support for the newly installed chief.

items.title: Breaking the raw material curse: How Techiman’s new cashew factory redefines Ghana’s export future
items.description: In a significant boost to Ghana’s industrialisation drive and agricultural value addition, President John Dramani Mahama has commissioned a state-of-the-art 100-metric-tonne-per-day cashew processing factory in Techiman, Bono East Region. The facility, funded by the Ghana Export-Import Bank (GEXIM) and operated by Nadkansco Processing Company Limited, represents a major leap forward in the country’s quest to move from raw material exportation to value-added processing for both local and international markets. Creating Jobs and Transforming Lives The impact on the local community is expected to be transformative. According to Belinda Akorfa Adokpa, Managing Director of Nadkansco Processing Company Limited, the factory will create 1,500 direct jobs and approximately 3,000 indirect jobs in the Techiman area and beyond. “This facility will generate foreign exchange and strengthen the local economy in Techiman and beyond,” Mrs. Adokpa stated during the commissioning ceremony. Beyond job creation, the company has demonstrated its commitment to community development by donating four new ambulances to four districts, including Atebubu, Wenchi, and Techiman North. Farmers in the region are set to be the highest beneficiaries, with the company committing to purchasing their cashew produce promptly, addressing a long-standing challenge of delayed payments that has plagued the agricultural sector. What This Means for the Local People For the residents of Techiman and surrounding communities, this factory represents more than just economic opportunity—it signals a new chapter of prosperity and self-sufficiency. Employment Opportunities With 1,500 direct jobs and 3,000 indirect jobs, thousands of families will have access to stable income, improving their standard of living and enabling them to invest in education, healthcare, and housing. Support for Local Farmers Cashew farmers in the region now have a reliable buyer for their produce. The guarantee of timely purchase eliminates the anxiety of post-harvest losses and provides farmers with the confidence to expand their cultivation. Economic Growth The injection of foreign exchange through export of processed cashew products will strengthen the local economy, leading to improved infrastructure, better services, and increased business opportunities for auxiliary industries. Healthcare Improvement The donation of four ambulances to Atebubu, Wenchi, and Techiman North districts will significantly improve emergency healthcare delivery, potentially saving lives that might otherwise be lost due to delayed medical response. Skills Development The factory will provide training and skills development opportunities for workers, equipping them with valuable expertise in agro-processing that can be transferred to other industries. Community Pride and Youth Retention The presence of a major industrial facility in the area will encourage young people to remain in the region rather than migrating to Accra and other cities in search of opportunities. Industry Stakeholder Reaction Samuel Amo Takyi, a respected stakeholder in the cashew industry, expressed enthusiasm about the development, describing the factory as a transformative investment for the region. “This new factory will go a long way to helping the local economy through agriculture,” Mr. Takyi said. “It is a super impact for Techiman, the region, and the country at large. This is exactly the kind of investment we need to unlock the full potential of Ghana’s cashew industry.” Government’s Commitment to Value Addition President Mahama, who was accompanied by the Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu Adjare, and other dignitaries, spoke passionately about the rationale behind his government’s focus on agribusiness. “The creation of the Agribusiness Ministry was to help with the processing of our locally produced foods for export purposes,” President Mahama explained. “We need to process more and consume our own foods. Export more means creating wealth and jobs. When you import, you are importing poverty.” The President announced that his government is investing 10 billion dollars of Ghana’s own money in eight sectors that will create jobs, with agriculture being one of the key sectors. GEXIM’s Role in Financing Productive Enterprises Sylvester Adinam Mensah, Chief Executive Officer of GEXIM, expressed excitement about the opportunities this company brings to the cashew industry and the country at large. “At Ghana Exim, our commitment remains clear: to finance productive enterprises, promote value addition, and position Ghana as a competitive player in global trade,” Mr. Mensah stated. Government Support and Policy Direction President Mahama assured Nadkansco of government support through GEXIM to enable the company to purchase sufficient cashew and preserve it for year-round operations. “I assure you that government will provide Nadkansco some funds through Ghana Exim to enable it buy enough cashew and preserve it so they run all year round,” the President promised. In a major policy shift aimed at promoting local processing, the President announced that Ghana is adopting a method already used by Ivory Coast. This will include: A ban on the export of raw cashew within the first three months of the new cashew season until local processors have secured enough raw materials A levy on exported cashew to discourage the exportation of raw nuts and promote value addition Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu Adjare, who is also the Member of Parliament for Techiman North, highlighted the benefits this company brings to her constituents. She emphasized the essential role her ministry is playing in ensuring that raw materials are always available to keep the company operational and urged the company to maintain good relationships with local farmers who supply raw materials. Call to Ghanaians President Mahama encouraged Ghanaians to venture into the manufacturing and agro-processing sectors rather than leaving it to foreigners. “We must not leave this to foreigners,” he urged. “Ghanaians should venture into manufacturing and agro-processing. This is how we create jobs for our people and build a prosperous nation.” The commissioning of the Nadkansco cashew processing factory marks a pivotal moment in Ghana’s journey toward industrialisation and agricultural transformation. For the people of Techiman and the Bono East Region, it represents hope, opportunity, and a brighter future. As the factory begins operations, it stands as a testament to what is possible when government, financial institutions, and private enterprise collaborate to create sustainable economic growth. The transformation from raw cashew exporter to value-added processor is not just an economic strategy—it is a pathway to prosperity for all Ghanaians.

items.title: AngloGold Ashanti Obuasi wins SSI Foundation Company of the Year
items.description: AngloGold Ashanti Obuasi Mine has received multiple honours at the 10th edition of the Sustainability and Social Investment (SSI) Awards, including the SSI Foundation Company of the Year award. The Mine also secured several corporate awards, while its Managing Director, Dr Ing. Sam Pobee, and Director of Sustainability Management, Edmund Oduro Agyei, received individual recognitions. Dr Pobee was named SSI Impact CEO of the Year for his leadership and commitment to responsible mining, sustainability and socio-economic development. Mr Oduro Agyei received the Sustainability Professional of the Year award for his work in advancing the Mine’s sustainability agenda through community development, strategic partnerships, economic empowerment and social investment. Commenting on the recognition, Mr Oduro Agyei said the awards reflected the collective efforts of the Mine, its employees, development partners and host communities. He linked the achievements to investments under the Mine’s Socio-Economic Development Plan (SEDP 2022–2031), which he said had contributed to improving livelihoods, strengthening local economies and expanding access to essential social services. He dedicated the awards to the Sustainability Management team and other stakeholders involved in advancing the Mine’s development agenda. Other corporate and individual awards AngloGold Ashanti Obuasi Mine also received awards in several categories, including: SSI Team of the Year Best Company in Economic Empowerment Best Company in Promoting Gender Inclusion and Diversity Best Company in Nature and Biodiversity Conservation and Protection Best Company in Community Development and Infrastructure Projects Best Company in Supporting Health Facilities and Institutions Best Company in Providing and Supporting Educational Facilities and Institutions Two other employees received individual honours. Phylis Quainoo was presented with the Diversity and Inclusion Leadership Impact Award, while Daniel Arthur Bentum received the Mentorship Leadership Impact Award. The recognitions cover areas including healthcare, education, community infrastructure, local enterprise development, gender inclusion and environmental protection. The Mine says its social investment programmes are intended to support socio-economic development in its host communities beyond its mining operations.

items.title: CAN 2027 : quatre heures d’attente à Alger, le Togo hausse le ton contre l’Algérie
items.description: Une nouvelle polémique oppose les fédérations togolaise et algérienne à la veille du deuxième rendez-vous entre les deux sélections. Le président de la Fédération togolaise de football (FTF), Guy Kossi Akpovy, accuse la partie algérienne de ne pas avoir facilité le départ de la délégation togolaise d’Alger, après la rencontre remportée par les Verts (1-0). Selon le dirigeant togolais, aucun représentant de la Fédération algérienne de football (FAF) n’était présent à l’aéroport international Houari-Boumédiène pour accompagner la délégation dans les formalités de départ. Dans une déclaration au quotidien algérien Compétition, Guy Kossi Akpovy a estimé que cette absence pouvait être intentionnelle. Aucun élément public ne permet toutefois, à ce stade, d’établir que le retard aurait été volontairement provoqué par la partie algérienne. Le président de la FTF explique que le Togo avait affrété un vol spécial, financé par le gouvernement, afin de permettre à sa sélection de regagner Lomé dans les meilleures conditions après le match disputé samedi en Algérie. L’avion aurait été disponible dès 2 heures du matin, tandis que la délégation togolaise serait arrivée à l’aéroport vers 3 heures. Pourtant, le décollage n’aurait finalement eu lieu qu’à 7 heures, soit environ quatre heures d’attente. Selon Akpovy, certains joueurs, particulièrement fatigués après la rencontre, auraient même dû dormir sur les sièges de l’aéroport en attendant le départ. « Ce n’est pas normal. Nous sommes dans le football » , a déploré le responsable togolais. Malgré son mécontentement, Guy Kossi Akpovy a assuré que la délégation algérienne ne ferait pas l’objet d’un traitement similaire lors de son déplacement à Lomé pour le match retour. De son côté, la Fédération algérienne de football n’a pas publiquement répondu à ces accusations à ce stade. Les circonstances exactes ayant entraîné le retard du vol restent donc à éclaircir. Les deux sélections doivent désormais se retrouver à Lomé pour la quatrième journée des éliminatoires. Une rencontre à fort enjeu pour les Togolais, qui chercheront à relancer leur campagne, tandis que l’Algérie tentera de conforter sa première place. items.title: At ECO moot, Dar calls for translating 'collective commitments into concrete action'
items.description: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar closed out the 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Ministers (COM) in Islamabad on Monday with a call for countries to translate their commitments into action. Pakistan, which holds the ECO chairmanship for 2026-27, hosted the meeting under the theme “Reviving Regionalism for a Resilient ECO”. The deputy premier, who chaired the meeting, expressed his “sincere appreciation to all delegations” for their constructive engagement during the meeting. “The deliberations today have reaffirmed our shared commitment to regional economic cooperation and integration,” Dar said. He termed the adoption of the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035 an “important milestone in charting the future course of our organisation over the next decade”, saying that it provided a shared framework to advance regional priorities alongside the Islamabad Communiqué. “Our task now is to translate our collective commitments into concrete action,” he added. “This will require clear priorities, realistic timelines, and effective follow-up mechanisms.” He highlighted regional cooperation as a central pillar of Pakistan’s foreign policy and noted that the country had consistently advocated a “stronger, more effective and responsive” ECO that harnessed “geographical proximity, historical bonds and economic complementarities”. Dar underscored Pakistan’s commitment to advancing the ECO agenda as the chair of the organisation and to working with all institutions and member states to strengthen regional connectivity, facilitate intra-regional trade and promote mutually beneficial economic cooperation. He looked forward to welcoming the countries back for the 31st COM meeting in 2027, saying, “Let us build on the momentum generated here so that our next meeting can take stock of tangible progress in advancing our shared priorities.” In addition, he wished Iran success in hosting the upcoming 18th ECO summit on Dec 3-4. The deputy premier thanked all member states, as well as the secretary general and his team, ECO permanent representatives, and senior officials for their support. Later in the day, Dar held a media briefing on the meeting alongside ECO Secretary General Asad Majeed Khan and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar. Joint communiqué The COM meeting concluded with the adoption of two documents, including the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035 and the Islamabad Communiqué. Pakistan’s mediation efforts hailed In the Islamabad Communiqué, ECO member states expressed concern over the “challenging geopolitical environment in the region, emphasising the importance of restraint, dialogue and diplomatic engagement, and recognising the important role” of Iran as a founding member of ECO. They expressed support for the mediation efforts undertaken by Pakistan and Qatar, as well as for the recent initiative put forward by Iran “aimed at achieving a dignified resolution of the conflict and ensuring the complete and permanent termination of the current war”. The ECO states commended Pakistan’s “consistent and constructive diplomatic support for ECO Member States and its mediation efforts towards de-escalation during the recent Iran-United States crisis”. They reaffirmed the importance of dialogue, diplomacy, respect for international law and promoting mutual trust. stability and the peaceful resolution of disputes, and calling for continued cooperation within the ECO framework towards lasting peace and stability in the region. The communiqué also highly appreciated Qatar’s “important role as a trusted facilitator of international diplomacy, most notably demonstrated by its mediation efforts at the 81st United Nations General Assembly”. The members commended ECO for “demonstrating that regionalism can remain effective and operational even under conditions of acute geopolitical stress”. The communiqué expressed concern over the humanitarian situation in Gaza after flooding on Nov 6 as winter begins. It urges priority delivery of food, medicine, fuel, heating equipment, tents, shelters, blankets and winter clothing. It also called for an immediate end to “policies of forced displacement and the deliberate deprivation of food” and full implementation of the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire agreement. The organisation rejected “unilateral coercive measures, sanctions and economic pressures and their extraterritorial economic, technological, financial or trade impacts”. It said they are contrary to the UN Charter and international law, adversely affect international peace and security, and undermine the provision of supply chains for food, pharmaceutical, energy and humanitarian assistance. The joint statement also mentioned Afghanistan, a member of the ECO, though seemingly not present at the meeting. ECO acknowledged the need for “continued consultation with member states to address the issues of Afghanistan’s engagement with the organisation in relevant areas, with a view to achieving the country’s full and effective participation once circumstances permit”. They stressed the need for “achieving meaningful progress on concerns of member states for fostering regional cooperation and laying the basis for Afghanistan’s participation in any ECO activities and processes”. Economy and trade The meeting expressed support for various documents adopted in the past, including ECO Vision 2025 and the 2021 Ashgabat Consensus for Action. They also welcomed various UN resolutions and initiatives. Members were urged to speed up amendment and implementation of the ECO Trade Agreement (ECOTA), with non-parties to the pact invited to consultations. The communique called for timely implementation of Turkmenistan’s feasibility study on the establishment of joint trade zones within the ECO region. They pointed to the Turkmenistan–Uzbekistan zone as a model and to a proposed trade market at the Altyn Asyr–Incheh Boroun border crossing between Iran and Turkmenistan. It urged joint measures on foreign direct investment, free economic zones, joint manufacturing, e-commerce and digitised customs “single window” systems. The ECO further stressed “expeditious conclusion” of the draft ECO Trade Facilitation Agreement and tasked the Joint Working Group with intensifying its technical negotiations toward the pact’s early finalisation. Pakistan has offered to host the 4th JWG meeting in the third quarter of 2026. The ministers called for more diversified financing, including through the ECO Trade and Development Bank (ECOTDB), whose membership they want expanded. Members were urged to fully implement the ECO Transit Transport Framework Agreement to “unlock the region’s full potential and enhance regional connectivity, trade, and economic development”. The ministers highlighted the ECO Sustainable and Resilient Transport Strategy 2026–2035 as a flagship framework. They also called for transport and transit corridors and better seaport access for landlocked members. The ECO members welcomed Shusha as ECO Tourism Capital 2026 and noted the schedule of future capitals: Lahore (2027), Mary (2028), Karakol (2029) and Aktau (2030). They also welcomed the operationalisation of the ECO Clean Energy Centre in Baku, as well as the “ECO Five-Year Roadmap on minerals cooperation for 2026–2030”, described as the first overarching framework for regional cooperation on minerals, including critical minerals. AI and technology The Islamabad Communiqué acknowledged UN actions on AI, including the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva on July 6–7. It underlined the need to bridge the AI capacity gap and promote “safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems in the non-military domain for sustainable development”. The statement also recognised the “transformative potential of emerging technologies”, such as AI, blockchain, quantum computing, 5G and robotics. It called for harnessing these technologies for regional prosperity, while noting the need to share experience on mitigating associated risks. Members were encouraged to cooperate on AI through exchanges of best practices, joint capacity-building and training under the ECO Science Foundation, aiming at bridging the “digital and artificial intelligence divide”. The ministers also noted the significance of the ECO Regional ICT Strategy 2026–2030, stressed the security of critical digital infrastructure, and called for cooperation among members in ICT security. They emphasised the “importance of ensuring equal, fair, transparent and non-discriminatory access, particularly for developing countries, to global markets for ICT security products, technologies and services, as a confidence-building measure”. The ECO members encouraged exploring cooperation on the peaceful uses of outer space, including satellite services, and space-based services in support of regional connectivity, disaster risk reduction and environmental monitoring. Araghchi calls for sustainable energy mechanism At the ECO meeting, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stressed the need for a reliable and sustainable regional energy mechanism during his address. The Iranian FM spoke about the US-Israeli war on Iran , which has also resulted in the choking of key fuel supply routes — the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab . “Our region needs not only an independent security framework but also a reliable and sustainable regional energy mechanism to safeguard energy flows, ensure stable supplies, reduce external vulnerabilities and enhance collective resilience against geopolitical shocks and disruptions,” Araghchi said, according to a transcript of his speech provided by the Iranian embassy in Pakistan. Araghchi said ECO was moving “beyond its traditional role towards becoming an effective platform for collective action, strengthened cooperation and joint efforts”. He said the shift would enable member states “to address emerging challenges and contribute to an inclusive and equitable global economic order”. He stressed the need for a “modern, new-generation, more inclusive, effective and operational trade agreement” that would benefit the region. Referring to the US war on Iran, Araghchi said, “Iran has remained committed to diplomatic engagement and peaceful solutions.” He added, however, that the US had opted for a different course of action, which was “marked by aggression, threats, targeted assassinations, economic coercion, and blockades, in flagrant violation of international law and the UN Charter”. He underscored that Iran had “no inherent dispute” with countries in the region, adding that “the territories, airspace and facilities of the regional countries must not be used as platforms for launching attacks against each other”. “Iran’s legitimate defensive measures are directed exclusively at the targets and military bases of the aggressors and should in no way be construed as actions against the peoples or governments of the neighbouring countries,” Araghchi said. He also called attention to Palestine , describing the genocide in Gaza as “the most pressing international crisis”. Condemning the destruction and killings at the hands of Israeli forces in Palestine, he said, “We are witnessing the intensification of expansionist policies by the Israeli regime in the West Bank and occupied Al-Quds.” “This is a moment that calls for concrete action, collective responsibility, and an end to silence and indifference.” He concluded his speech by reiterating that Iran’s stability and prosperity were “intrinsically linked” to those of other ECO members. ECO delegation heads call on PM Shehbaz Separately, the foreign ministers and delegation heads of ECO member states paid a joint call on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, according to a handout issued by the PM’s Office. The premier thanked them for their participation in the meeting and reaffirmed Pakistan’s “strong commitment” to ECO objectives. He reiterated his government’s resolve to promote regional cooperation, connectivity and economic integration within the ECO member states. The premier appreciated the meeting’s successful conclusion and welcomed the adoption of the Islamabad Communique and the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035, describing them as “important steps” towards strengthening the organisation and advancing shared regional priorities. The premier highlighted Pakistan’s ECO chairmanship and emphasised the need to translate the organisation’s collective vision into concrete, result-oriented initiatives that deliver “tangible benefits” to the region’s people. Furthermore, the handout said that the premier called for enhanced cooperation in trade and investment, transport and transit connectivity, energy, information and communication technology, and sustainable development. “He stressed the importance of effective implementation of existing ECO agreements and strengthening institutional mechanisms to accelerate regional economic integration,” the statement said. PM Shehbaz highlighted the country’s strategic geographical location. He reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to enhancing regional connectivity through road, rail and multimodal transport corridors, including linkages with the ports of Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar, to facilitate access to regional and international markets, particularly for landlocked ECO member states. “Underlining Pakistan’s commitment to dialogue and diplomacy for the peaceful resolution of disputes, the premier stressed the importance of collective efforts to address threats to regional security,” the statement added. He also expressed Pakistan’s resolve to work closely with all member states and the ECO secretariat to further strengthen the organisation during its chairmanship. “The prime minister reaffirmed that Pakistan looked forward to welcoming ECO member states again in 2027 for the next Council of Ministers Meeting and the ECO summit,” the handout concluded. Dar holds sideline meetings with participating dignitaries The deputy premier also held separate meetings with ministers from several countries attending the ECO moot. With FM Araghchi , Dar emphasised that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means of addressing outstanding issues, preventing escalation and achieving lasting peace and stability, the Foreign Office said. Meanwhile, Tajikistan’s FM Sirojiddin Muhriddin and Dar reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation within ECO and advancing its regional priorities. According to FO, the Tajik minister appreciated Pakistan’s warm hospitality. The two leaders “underscored the importance of realising the full potential of bilateral trade” and also discussed advancing energy cooperation, particularly through the early operationalisation of CASA-1000 . Dar and Turkiye’s Deputy FM Musa Kulaklikaya reaffirmed their “commitment to further strengthening the longstanding bonds of friendship and brotherhood” between their countries, FO said. Dar thanked Türkiye for its active participation in the Council of Ministers meeting, while Kulaklikaya thanked Pakistan for the warm hospitality and arrangements for the meeting. In his meeting with Dar, Kyrgyz Republic’s Deputy FM Kairat Tursunkulov delivered a letter from Foreign Minister Zheenbek Kulubaev, “reaffirming the close bonds of friendship and commitment to advancing bilateral ties”, FO said. The two sides discussed strengthening bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and connectivity, and emphasised the importance of continued cooperation under ECO. Pakistan calls on Afghanistan to address terror concerns In his opening speech at the meeting, Dar said Pakistan desired a peaceful, prosperous and stable Afghanistan , but meaningful progress towards regional cooperation required the Afghan authorities to address the legitimate security concerns of neighbouring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism. He added that a stable Afghanistan, at peace with itself and all its neighbours and fully integrated into the ECO framework, would benefit the Afghan people as well as the wider region by opening up avenues for trade, transit and economic cooperation. “At the same time, meaningful progress requires the Afghan authorities to address the legitimate security concerns of the neighbouring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism,” Dar said. He stressed that a secure and stable environment was essential for sustained regional economic partnerships, adding that these considerations remained central to Pakistan’s broader connectivity agenda. “Regional connectivity rests on more than the routes that link us. It depends upon trust between states and confidence that international commitments will be honoured. Unresolved disputes and the non-fulfilment of international obligations can erode that trust and impede economic progress,” said Dar. The foreign minister emphasised that respect for international law and treaties is essential to enduring economic partnerships between countries. Outlining Pakistan’s priorities during its chairmanship of the ECO, Dar identified five key areas of focus, including expanding trade and investment, strengthening regional connectivity, advancing the ECO Trade Agreement, building regional resilience and promoting human development. The foreign minister said the region’s natural resources, energy reserves, agricultural potential and strategic location offered considerable opportunities for economic cooperation, but realising that potential required functioning transport corridors, efficient border procedures and predictable transit arrangements. He said Pakistan would work towards wider market access, stronger regional value chains and greater private sector participation, particularly by small and medium-sized enterprises, to boost trade and investment among member states. “Closer interaction among our business communities can help translate commercial potential into greater trade and investment.” Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in a cordial exchange with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Tajikistan Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin, OIC Secretary General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed and ECO Secretary General Dr. Asad Majeed Khan on the sidelines of the 30th ECO Council of Ministers Meeting in Islamabad on Nov 16. — ForeignOfficePk/X On connectivity, Dar said Pakistan would seek to improve transport and transit links between Central Asia, South Asia and Pakistani ports on the Arabian Sea. Harmonised customs procedures, efficient border management and predictable transit arrangements were essential to making regional trade routes commercially viable, he added. The foreign minister also highlighted the need to advance the ECO Trade Agreement, saying the negotiating strategy and roadmap approved by ECO trade ministers in November 2025 provided a basis for modernising the agreement. Pakistan would support efforts to develop a more effective, inclusive and digitally enabled regional trade framework, he said. On regional resilience, Dar called for closer cooperation in disaster preparedness, early warning systems, sustainable water management and climate-resilient infrastructure, noting that climate change and growing pressure on water and energy resources posed serious challenges to regional economies. He also underscored the importance of human development, particularly in education, research, innovation and vocational training, saying greater opportunities in these areas could equip young people with skills needed by changing economies. Promoting entrepreneurship and professional exchanges would further strengthen regional integration, he added. The foreign minister maintained that the five priorities were interconnected and their success would depend on collective efforts by member states. He expressed Pakistan’s readiness to work with ECO members and the organisation’s secretariat on initiatives relating to trade facilitation, transit connectivity and disaster preparedness. Regional peace and diplomatic efforts Dar cautioned that peace and stability were essential for economic development, warning that conflict and insecurity in the region could disrupt trade routes, energy supplies, investment and economic projects. “Peace and development reinforce each other,” he said. He added that Pakistan remained “deeply concerned about conflict and instability” in the region. “Their consequences extend beyond national boundaries, disrupting trade routes, energy supplies, investment, and the economic projects of our peoples.” He said that Pakistan has consistently advocated for “the peaceful resolution of disputes through dialogue and diplomacy in accordance with international law and the United Nations Charter”. Referring to Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts in the US-Israeli war on Iran, Dar said, “Pakistan will continue these diplomatic efforts in support of dialogue, de-escalation, and lasting regional stability.” He said that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir “remained closely engaged with brotherly countries and international partners to facilitate peaceful outcomes”. Senior officials meet to finalise agenda Senior officials of the ECO finalised the agenda and draft Islamabad Communiqué on Sunday, ahead of the organisation’s COM meeting. According to a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA), the Senior Officials Meeting (SOM) was held on Nov 15 under the chairmanship of Foreign Secretary Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad. The meeting was attended by senior officials from ECO member states, representatives of the ECO Secretariat, and delegates from the organisation’s specialised agencies and regional institutions. The officials reviewed preparations for the ministerial meeting and finalised its agenda and the draft Islamabad Communiqué for consideration by the foreign ministers. They also reviewed the activities undertaken by the ECO Secretariat during the year, including ongoing programmes and initiatives, outcomes of sectoral ministerial meetings, and the work of subsidiary bodies and specialised institutions, the ministry said. Administrative and financial matters of the organisation also came under discussion, with participants exchanging views on measures to improve its effectiveness. The SOM serves as a preparatory forum for the ECO COM, enabling member states to assess progress, discuss issues of mutual interest and build consensus on proposals and draft documents ahead of ministerial-level deliberations.

items.title: Open Letter To the Government: Who’s protecting young Ghanaians travelling to Russia? Are they safe?
items.description: Dear President John Dramani Mahama and Honourable Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, Minister for Foreign Affairs, I write as a concerned Ghanaian journalist, increasingly worried about reports of young Ghanaians being lured into the Russia-Ukraine war, with some losing their lives, others ending up as prisoners of war and several more remaining missing. My concern is not about Ghana’s diplomatic relations with Russia or an attempt to discourage legitimate educational and employment opportunities abroad, in general. It is about the responsibility of government to protect Ghanaian citizens, particularly young people who may be vulnerable to deception and exploitation. My question is simple but urgent: What specific safety and security alerts are being given to young Ghanaians travelling to Russia, particularly students and beneficiaries of scholarship programmes, to ensure they do not become victims of recruitment networks allegedly luring foreigners into the war? This question has become even more pertinent following the disturbing revelations about Ghanaians who have died or gone missing in the conflict and the recent departure of scholarship beneficiaries to Russia. The frightening numbers we cannot ignore This is no longer speculation. Ghana’s own Foreign Affairs Minister, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, has repeatedly confirmed the scale of the problem following engagements with Ukrainian authorities. In February 2026, following his visit to Ukraine, the Minister disclosed that at least 55 Ghanaians had been killed while fighting in the Russia-Ukraine war, with two others being held as prisoners of war. Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha‎ and his Ghanaian counterpart Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa paid their respects to those killed in the war. He also revealed that approximately 272 Ghanaians had been lured into the conflict since 2022 through transnational recruitment networks. Across Africa, an estimated 1,780 people from 36 countries were believed to have been recruited to fight for Russia. Ghana’s Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Ablakwa met with some Ghanaian prisoners of war in Ukraine. Some of the affected Ghanaians were reportedly attracted by opportunities advertised as civilian employment, including construction, hospitality, logistics and security jobs, only to find themselves involved in the war. The situation became even more troubling in August 2026 when Mr Ablakwa disclosed that the number of Ghanaians killed had risen to 62, with another 15 missing. Read Also: 62 Ghanaians killed, 15 missing in Russia-Ukraine war – Ablakwa Speaking during his visit to Russia, the Minister reiterated Ghana’s concerns and efforts to engage Russian authorities to address the situation. His position was particularly emphatic: “This is not our war, and it should not be claiming Ghanaian lives.” These are not merely statistics. They represent families whose sons, brothers, husbands and relatives may never return home. They represent young people who may have travelled in search of better economic opportunities but ended up fighting in a war in which Ghana has no stake. The government must therefore move beyond expressing concern and prioritise preventive measures. John Dumelo’s scholarship initiative: An opportunity, but are the necessary precautions being taken? My immediate concern was heightened by the recent announcement by the Member of Parliament for Ayawaso West Wuogon and Deputy Minister for Food and Agriculture, John Dumelo, that the first batch of beneficiaries under his scholarship initiative had departed Ghana for Russia to pursue further studies. The initiative is expected to support more than 40 students by the end of 2027. The effort could be viewed as commendable. At a time when many Ghanaian families struggle to finance tertiary education, providing young people with opportunities to study abroad deserves recognition. MP for Ayawaso West Wuogon. John Dumelo in a shot with the 1st batch of students going to Russia. However, while I welcomed the announcement, I could not help but ask some uncomfortable questions. What happens when these young people arrive in Russia? Who takes responsibility for their safety beyond providing scholarships and admission arrangements? Have they received adequate security orientation about the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and reports of foreign nationals being lured into the Russian military? Have they been warned about individuals or organisations that may approach them with attractive financial offers, employment opportunities or promises of a better life in exchange for signing military contracts? Do they know that some Ghanaians reportedly travelled to Russia for civilian employment but eventually ended up on the battlefield? Have their sponsors established reliable channels through which their welfare can be monitored throughout their stay? And have their parents and guardians been informed about the potential risks and provided with emergency contacts should anything go wrong? I raise these questions without suggesting that Mr Dumelo’s scholarship initiative is connected in any way to the reported recruitment activities. There is no basis for such an allegation. My concern is that a good educational opportunity can become a vulnerable entry point for exploitation if beneficiaries are not adequately prepared and protected. The fact that these young people are travelling primarily to study does not automatically make them immune to approaches by individuals seeking to exploit their financial circumstances, ambitions or unfamiliarity with the country. I would therefore expect that every Ghanaian public official, institution or individual facilitating educational opportunities in Russia works closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ghana’s diplomatic mission to ensure that beneficiaries receive proper security briefings before departure. The question is whether we are doing enough to ensure they return safely after completing their studies. Ghana-Russia labour recruitment agreement: Are adequate safeguards in place? My concerns are further heightened by another development reported by Citi Newsroom on October 29, 2026. According to the report, Ghana signed an agreement with Russia to facilitate the recruitment of Ghanaian workers for industrial and manufacturing jobs. The agreement was signed by Labour Minister Emmanuel Agyekum and the director of Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone, an industrial hub comprising 48 companies with a reported requirement for more than 75,000 workers. Alabuga is a name known to many. Stories have been published about young women being tricked into going to Alabuga to work in drone factories used by Russia to attack Ukraine. Under the arrangement, Ghana’s Labour Ministry is expected to coordinate recruitment, verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation to safeguard the interests of Ghanaian workers. Ghana’s Labour Minister Emmanuel Agyekum & Director of Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone, E.R. Safuillin, signing the pact. While creating legitimate employment opportunities for young Ghanaians is commendable, the timing of this agreement raises important questions that the government must address. Considering the disturbing reports of Ghanaians being lured to Russia with promises of lucrative civilian employment before allegedly ending up on the battlefield, what additional safeguards have been incorporated into this agreement to prevent a recurrence? What specific companies will employ the Ghanaian workers, what jobs will they perform, and who will independently verify their employment contracts and working conditions? Will the government ensure that every prospective worker understands the nature of the job, the terms of engagement, their rights and the procedures for leaving employment should the circumstances differ from what was promised? More importantly, what guarantees exist that these workers will not be approached, pressured or deceived into signing military contracts after arriving in Russia? The Labour Minister’s assurance that the Ministry will verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation is important. But given what Ghana has already experienced, I believe the government must go further by establishing independent monitoring, accessible complaint mechanisms and clear protections against any attempt to recruit these workers into military service. We cannot be facilitating the movement of Ghanaian workers to Russia through official government arrangements without first demonstrating that we have put adequate safeguards in place to protect them. The opportunity to work abroad should never become a pathway to a foreign battlefield. Ukraine’s warning should not be taken lightly Ghana has received warnings from Ukrainian authorities about the dangers facing its citizens in Russia. During his February 2026 visit to Kyiv, Mr Ablakwa held discussions with his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, who raised concerns about the recruitment of African nationals into the Russian military. The Ukrainian Foreign Minister warned that Africans, including Ghanaians, were being drawn into the conflict through deceptive recruitment arrangements. More recently, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, addressing the 81st United Nations General Assembly in September 2026, identified Ghana among 47 countries whose citizens, he said, were being used in Russia’s war against Ukraine. Read Also: ‘Do not let Russia pay for its madness with lives of your people’ – Zelensky to Ghana, 46 other countries He urged the affected countries to protect their nationals and prevent them from ending up on the battlefield, highlighting the use of deception and other tactics to recruit foreign nationals. Ghana was specifically mentioned. What more warning does our government need to appreciate the urgency of this situation? Is Ghana doing enough to alert prospective travellers? The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has previously issued travel advisories cautioning Ghanaians against travelling to conflict areas and warning them about middlemen and agents who promise employment and other opportunities in countries experiencing armed conflict. But the circumstances have since become even more alarming. We now have official figures indicating that dozens of Ghanaians have died, others are missing, and some have been captured as prisoners of war. The question is whether the Ministry has moved beyond general travel advisories to a targeted and sustained public education campaign addressing the dangers facing Ghanaians travelling to Russia. How many prospective students are aware of the reported recruitment tactics? How many scholarship beneficiaries have been reached? How many travel agencies, universities and educational facilitators have been engaged? And how many parents and guardians have been sensitised? It is not enough for the Ministry to issue statements on its website or social media platforms and assume that everyone who needs the information has received it. A warning is only useful when it reaches the people it is intended to protect. It is also important to acknowledge that Russia has rejected allegations of deliberately recruiting African nationals unlawfully into its military. Russian Ambassador to Ghana, Andrei Ordash, has maintained that foreign nationals can voluntarily enlist through contractual arrangements under Russian law. However, the concern is not simply that a Ghanaian may voluntarily choose to join a foreign military. It is that people travelling in search of legitimate civilian employment or educational opportunities could allegedly be deceived, coerced or manipulated into participating in a war. Ghana cannot leave the protection of its citizens entirely to assurances from foreign governments. Putin’s assurance: Is that enough? At the recent Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, President John Dramani Mahama raised Ghana’s concerns about recruiting its citizens into the Russia-Ukraine war during bilateral discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin. According to the Ghanaian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, President Putin gave an assurance that Ghanaians would no longer be permitted to participate in the war. The commitment, as communicated by the Ghanaian government, is expected to address both irregular recruitment arrangements and voluntary enlistment. The development is welcome, and President Mahama deserves commendation for raising an issue that has caused so much pain to Ghanaian families. However, is President Putin’s assurance sufficient reason for Ghana to relax its vigilance and allow its citizens, particularly young people, to continue travelling to Russia without comprehensive security education and precautionary measures? I do not think so. A diplomatic assurance, however significant, must be followed by practical measures, monitoring and accountability. The government must also ensure that recruitment networks allegedly operating to lure unsuspecting Africans are identified and dismantled. What happens to the 15 Ghanaians reported missing? What about those already in captivity or serving in the Russian military? How will Ghana verify that the commitment announced after the summit is being implemented? What I expect the government to do Mr President and Honourable Minister, I believe the time has come for Ghana to introduce a more deliberate security education programme for all Ghanaians travelling to Russia. Specifically, I would respectfully suggest the following: Mandatory pre-departure security briefings: Every Ghanaian travelling to Russia for education, employment, or an extended stay should receive an official briefing on the conflict, deceptive recruitment tactics, suspicious employment offers and the dangers of signing unfamiliar military contracts. Special protection for scholarship beneficiaries: The Ministry should work with MPs, scholarship sponsors, universities and educational agencies to ensure that beneficiaries are properly briefed, registered and provided with emergency contacts before departure. A targeted public travel advisory: Ghana needs a clear, regularly updated advisory addressing the specific dangers of deceptive recruitment in Russia, widely circulated through traditional media, social media, universities and district assemblies. Citizens should be made aware of places like Alabuga and its mission to build drones for Russia’s war in Ukraine. Monitoring of Ghanaian students and workers: Ghana’s diplomatic mission should maintain an effective registration system and conduct regular welfare checks on Ghanaians living in Russia. Investigation of recruitment networks: The relevant security agencies should identify and investigate individuals and organisations suspected of facilitating deceptive recruitment into foreign military service. A dedicated emergency reporting mechanism: Ghanaians in Russia and their families back home should have an accessible channel for reporting suspicious recruitment, coercion, disappearance and other threats to their safety. Monitoring of the Putin commitment: Ghana should establish a concrete follow-up arrangement with Russian authorities to verify that the announced commitment is being implemented and that violations are investigated. These measures are not intended to discourage legitimate educational or economic relations with Russia. They are intended to ensure that such relations do not expose Ghanaian citizens to preventable dangers. Our young people deserve opportunities, but above all, they deserve protection Ghana has every right to pursue diplomatic, economic and educational partnerships with Russia. There is nothing inherently wrong with Ghanaian students travelling there to acquire knowledge, build careers and contribute to national development. But we must not let the excitement around international opportunities overshadow the realities confronting some of our citizens. When 62 Ghanaians have reportedly died, and 15 others are missing in a foreign war, we cannot afford to treat the matter as an ordinary diplomatic disagreement. When the Ukrainian President has specifically mentioned Ghana among countries whose citizens are allegedly being lured into the conflict, our response must go beyond statements of concern. And when our own Foreign Affairs Minister acknowledges that criminal networks are exploiting young Ghanaians through deceptive employment arrangements, the government must ensure that prospective travellers understand those dangers before leaving the country. I am particularly worried that, in our enthusiasm to promote international educational opportunities, we may be overlooking the need to educate young people about the security implications of travelling to a country involved in an active war. A scholarship should be an opportunity to acquire an education, not an avenue through which a young person becomes vulnerable to exploitation. A job offer should provide an opportunity to earn a living, not become a deceptive pathway to the battlefield. Mr President and Honourable Minister, Ghanaians should not have to choose between pursuing opportunities abroad and remaining safe. The government must find a way to guarantee both. My question, therefore, remains: Following the deaths, disappearances and imprisonment of several Ghanaians in the Russia-Ukraine war, what specific safety and security alerts are being given to young Ghanaians travelling to Russia today, and what concrete measures are in place to ensure they are not lured into this war? President Putin may have given his assurance, but can Ghana afford to simply look on and watch its young people travel to Russia without first ensuring that they understand the risks and know how to protect themselves? I believe the answer should be an emphatic no. We have already lost too many lives. We should not wait for another Ghanaian family to receive devastating news before taking preventive action. The government’s responsibility is not only to negotiate the safe return of citizens who have fallen victim to dangerous circumstances. It is also to prevent more citizens from becoming victims in the first place. Our young people deserve opportunities. But above all, they deserve to live long enough to benefit from them. Yours in the interest of Ghana and the protection of its citizens,

items.title: CAN 2027, Togo-Algérie : sept blessés en un seul stage, Hemdani répond à la polémique
items.description: Sept blessés durant un seul stage ! L’équipe d’Algérie a perdu sept joueurs depuis le début du stage pour la double confrontation contre le Togo en éliminatoires de la CAN 2027. Cinq joueurs ont déclaré forfait avant la première manche samedi au stade de Hocine Aït Ahmed de Tizi-Ouzou. Il s’agit des défenseurs Jaouen Hadjam et Rafik Belghali, du milieu de terrain Hicham Boudaoui et des attaquants Bachir Belloumi et Amin Chiakha. Après le match Algérie – Togo (1-0), deux éléments clés du dispositif de Brahim Hemdani ont rejoint la liste, déjà longue, des blessés : les attaquants Ibrahim Maza et Anis Hadj Moussa . Équipe d’Algérie : un nombre inédit de blessés en un seul stage Face à cette hécatombe, une polémique a éclaté sur les réseaux sociaux. Un certain malaise commence à s’installer autour de la sélection nationale. Certains soupçonnent les joueurs de simuler les blessures pour éviter d’effectuer des déplacements périlleux en Afrique, d’autres évoquent une charge de travail excessive à l’entraînement des Fennecs. Interrogé ce lundi sur le nombre de joueurs blessés inédit enregistré en un seul stage des Fennecs, le sélectionneur national Brahim Hemdani a répondu. « Les blessures ne sont pas dues à la charge d’entraînement, qui est parfaitement calculée et individualisée. On a sept blessés. Beaucoup de sélections ont des blessés. Les types de blessures peuvent être musculaires ou articulaires. En tout cas, cela n’a pas été lié à une charge d’entraînement excessive », a-t-il déclaré, la veille du deuxième match face au Togo demain mardi 17 novembre à Lomé (17 h 00). Pour le match face au Togo mardi à Lomé, il est resté vague : « Tous les matchs en Afrique sont compliqués à jouer. » L’article CAN 2027, Togo-Algérie : sept blessés en un seul stage, Hemdani répond à la polémique est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: GSSTI Director urges passage of national space law to unlock Ghana’s share of US$680bn space economy
items.description: The Director of the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI), Dr Joseph Tandoh, has called for the urgent establishment of the Ghana Space Agency and the passage of a national space law to regulate the country’s space activities, protect national interests and unlock economic opportunities in the global space industry. He said although Ghana had made progress in developing its space policy and securing Cabinet approval for the proposed agency, the absence of an operational regulatory framework was delaying the country’s ability to fully participate in the rapidly expanding space economy. Speaking on the sidelines of the 2026 Ghana Space Conference in Accra on Monday, November 16, Dr Tandoh said Ghana needed to move from policy development to implementation to position itself to benefit from the opportunities in space science and technology. He recalled Ghana’s achievement in 2017 when All Nations University launched GhanaSat, which generated national excitement and demonstrated the country’s capacity to participate in space-related activities. He said Ghana also began developing its national space policy that year, which was subsequently approved by Cabinet in 2022 and unveiled in 2024. Cabinet further approved the establishment of the Ghana Space Agency in 2025, but Dr Tandoh stressed that the approval did not mean the institution had formally been established. He said the 2026 conference, running from November 16 to 18, was therefore intended to build understanding of why Ghana needed the agency, its responsibilities and the legal framework required to make it operational. Dr Tandoh identified three major reasons for establishing the agency: protecting the country, generating economic benefits and building national capacity in space science and technology. On national protection, he warned that Ghana currently lacked the necessary legal framework to address liabilities and regulate space activities, including incidents involving falling rocket debris or damage caused by space objects. He noted that although Ghana had signed international instruments such as the Outer Space Treaty, the Rescue Agreement and the Liability Convention, the country had yet to ratify them. He said the situation raised questions about which institution would be responsible for handling space-related incidents and ensuring that Ghana’s interests were protected. Dr Tandoh also expressed concern about the absence of a regulatory authority to supervise space activities undertaken by universities, private companies and start-ups. He explained that under the Outer Space Treaty, countries are responsible for authorising and supervising space activities conducted within their territories, whether by government institutions or private entities. He said the proposed Ghana Space Agency would provide the institutional framework to discharge these responsibilities, making the development and passage of a national space bill particularly urgent. On the economic opportunities, Dr Tandoh said the global space economy was valued at approximately US$680 billion and grew by 12 per cent in the previous year, generating an estimated US$2 billion daily. He questioned how Ghana intended to position itself to capture a share of the growing industry, particularly given its geographical location along the Equator. According to him, Ghana’s location offers a strategic advantage for launching rockets into space at potentially lower costs, making the country an attractive destination for companies exploring spaceport development. He disclosed that several companies had expressed interest in exploring opportunities to establish spaceports in Ghana but stressed that the absence of clear laws and regulations remained a major obstacle to attracting such investments. Dr Tandoh said enacting the necessary legislation would provide the certainty investors needed to commit resources to the country’s space industry. He also called on Members of Parliament and relevant government ministries to support the proposed space bill when it is presented to Parliament, describing it as essential to Ghana’s development. On capacity building, he said satellite technology had important applications in mining, natural resource management and national security, making it necessary for Ghana to develop its own expertise and technical capabilities. He argued that the country could not continue relying heavily on foreign partners for satellite imagery and other space-based information, particularly when it needed data to address its own development challenges. “Nobody understands our problems better than we do, and we cannot always depend on foreign partners for satellite images,” he said. Dr Tandoh said establishing the Ghana Space Agency, backed by appropriate legislation, would help coordinate the country’s space activities, attract investment and equip the next generation of Ghanaian professionals with the skills needed to compete in the industry. He said Ghana must act decisively to ensure it was not left behind as the global space economy expanded. “Our message is simple: Let us establish the Ghana Space Agency, back it up with the necessary regulations to make it work, and empower the agency to build the capacity of the next generation of space science and technology professionals we need,” he added.

items.title: Space Hubs Africa urges coordinated approach to make Ghana a key player in Africa’s space industry
items.description: The Director of Space Hubs Africa, Kwaku Sumah, has called for a coordinated national approach to space science and technology, urging Ghana to move beyond discussions and translate its space ambitions into practical outcomes that benefit citizens. He said the establishment of the proposed Ghana Space Agency presented an opportunity to organise the country’s growing space ecosystem, bring stakeholders together and position Ghana as a major player in Africa’s space industry. Speaking on the sidelines of the 2026 Ghana Space Conference in Accra on Monday, November 16, Mr Sumah said this year’s edition, themed From Vision to Action, was focused on identifying practical measures to ensure the agency meets the expectations and development needs of Ghanaians. He noted that while last year’s conference concentrated on defining Ghana’s aspirations for the space sector, the focus had shifted to implementation following Cabinet approval for the formation of the Ghana Space Agency. “This year, however, we’ve decided there’s enough talking. It is time to take action,” he said, adding that Ghana must seize the opportunity to establish itself as a key player in the African space industry. The three-day conference, running from November 16 to 18, has brought together representatives from government ministries, Ghana’s military services, scientists, technology professionals, entrepreneurs and students to discuss the country’s space priorities. Mr Sumah said the discussions were expected to produce an Accra Declaration 2026, capturing the needs and recommendations of different sectors to guide the proposed agency. The document, he explained, would be presented to the Attorney-General’s Office, the Office of the Presidency and relevant ministries to ensure the agency is established with the needs of the people and institutions at its core. He identified inadequate coordination among individuals and organisations working in Ghana’s space sector as one of the major challenges identified during the previous conference. However, he said there had since been improvements, citing growing partnerships between the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI), the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO) and the Ghana Navy. He also welcomed increasing participation by students and other Ghanaians, stressing the need to sustain the momentum through stronger institutional and individual collaboration. On the benefits of investing in space technology, Mr Sumah said satellite applications went beyond astronauts and space exploration, offering practical solutions to everyday challenges, including flooding, disaster management, communications and natural resource monitoring. Using the recent Accra floods as an example, he explained that satellite technology could help authorities predict rainfall and identify vulnerable communities before disasters occur. During flooding, satellite imagery could map affected areas, identify locations at risk and support evacuation planning, while post-disaster mapping could help assess damage and improve urban planning to prevent future occurrences. He described satellite data as an important tool for improving decision-making across several sectors, including security, environmental management and natural resource protection. Mr Sumah further highlighted three major applications of satellite technology: navigation, communication and Earth observation. He explained that satellite navigation already supports everyday services such as Uber, Yango and Bolt by providing location and direction information to users. Satellite communication, he said, could help extend connectivity over long distances and improve access to communication services in rural and underserved communities. Earth observation, meanwhile, involves capturing images of the planet from space to monitor activities on the ground, track environmental changes and support disaster response. He said the technology could provide detailed imagery, with resolutions of up to three metres, allowing authorities to monitor developments and make better-informed decisions. Mr Sumah urged Ghanaians to recognise that satellite technology was already relevant to their daily lives and that the country needed a deliberate strategy to maximise its growing applications. He said the industry would continue to evolve, making it important for Ghana to build local capacity, encourage innovation and ensure that citizens, particularly young people, had opportunities to participate. “Space is for everyone. Satellite technology is for everyone,” he said, calling for a coordinated effort among government, industry, academia and citizens to harness the technology for national development.

items.description: À deux semaines de la première édition du Forum international des chargeurs africains (FICA), prévue du 30 novembre au 2 décembre à Dakar, le Conseil sénégalais des chargeurs (COSEC) intensifie ses démarches auprès de ses partenaires continentaux. Une délégation conduite par son directeur général, Ousseynou Pouye, est en mission à Conakry depuis lundi pour préparer la participation guinéenne à cette rencontre et les travaux de l’Union des conseils des chargeurs africains (UCCA). Le Sénégal poursuit ses consultations avec les acteurs africains du secteur du transport et de la logistique en prélude au FICA 2026. Dans cette dynamique, une délégation du Conseil sénégalais des chargeurs (COSEC), conduite par son directeur général, Ousseynou Pouye, effectue une mission de travail à Conakry auprès du Conseil guinéen des chargeurs (CGC). Accueillie à l’aéroport international Ahmed Sékou Touré par Lancinè Keita, directeur général du CGC et vice-président de l’UCCA, la délégation sénégalaise entend notamment échanger avec son partenaire guinéen sur les modalités de participation au Forum, qui se tiendra à l’hôtel King Fahd Palace de Dakar. Cette première édition du FICA réunira, du 30 novembre au 2 décembre, les acteurs du secteur autour du thème : « Compétitivité et résilience des chaînes logistiques africaines : le chargeur au cœur de la ZLECAf ». En marge de cette rencontre, se tiendra également le Comité directeur de l’UCCA. Les échanges entre les deux institutions portent ainsi sur la participation de la Guinée à ces deux rendez-vous et la préparation des travaux statutaires de l’Union. Pour Ousseynou Pouye, cette coopération repose sur des préoccupations communes aux conseils des chargeurs du continent. « Nos deux conseils partagent les mêmes défis et la même ambition : des chargeurs mieux défendus, des corridors plus fluides et des échanges facilités entre nos pays, dans l'esprit de la ZLECAf », a-t-il déclaré. La mission de Conakry s'inscrit dans une série de démarches diplomatiques et institutionnelles engagées par le COSEC pour assurer une participation africaine à la hauteur des ambitions du Forum. Du 8 au 10 novembre, son directeur général avait effectué une visite à Praia, au Cap-Vert, où il avait remis aux autorités capverdiennes l'invitation officielle au FICA 2026. Le pays est désigné invité d'honneur de cette première édition. À travers ces consultations, le COSEC entend consolider les partenariats entre les conseils des chargeurs africains et promouvoir une meilleure prise en compte de leurs préoccupations dans les politiques de transport et de facilitation des échanges. Cette démarche s'inscrit dans les orientations nationales en matière de coopération africaine et de souveraineté logistique, portées par les autorités sénégalaises. À l'approche du rendez-vous de Dakar, l'enjeu est désormais de réunir les institutions et les professionnels du secteur autour de réponses communes aux défis de compétitivité, de fluidité des corridors et d'intégration des chaînes logistiques africaines.
